#4684. What is Gonzo? We asked three biologists.

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 13, 2026 9:39 AM EST

Many of the Muppets are pretty easy to pin down, species-wise. Kermit is a frog. Fozzie is a bear. Miss Piggy is, obviously, a feisty piggy. But Gonzo—with his blue-ish fur, bulging eyes, tuft of purple feathers, and long, curved nose that looks a little like a beak—is something of an enigma. The writers of the Muppets have avoided the question of what Gonzo is for years.

Well, in a new episode of Popular Science’s Ask Us Anything podcast, we asked three biologists to break down exactly what Gonzo is. We also talk to Muppets legend and Gonzo performer Dave Goelz to get his take.

Ask Us Anything answers your most outlandish, mind-burning questions—from the everyday things you’ve always wondered to the bizarre things you never thought to ask. So, yes, there’s a reason candy tastes different now and no, you don’t need to worry about Yellowstone’s supervolcano blowing up anytime soon. If you have a question for us, send us a note. Nothing is too silly or simple.

This episode is based on the Popular Science article “What kind of animal is Gonzo?”

Listen and follow Ask Us Anything on your favorite podcast platform:

Spotify | Apple Podcasts | YouTube | Or wherever you get your podcasts.

Sarah Durn: Picture some of the most recognizable characters from The Muppets. Maybe you’re thinking of Kermit the Frog, or Miss Piggy, or Fozzie Bear. But today, we’re talking about a Muppet who’s a little harder to describe: Gonzo. You know the one. He’s got bluish fur, big bulging eyes, a tuft of purple feathers on his head, and a long curved nose that looks a little like a beak.

You might know him as The Great Gonzo, the fearless daredevil, performance artist, and stunt Muppet who eats tires, catches cannonballs bare-handed, and courts his beloved Camilla, who is a chicken. So yeah, Gonzo is a pretty unusual guy. But here’s something you might never have stopped to think about. What exactly is Gonzo?

Is he a bird, a lizard, an alien? All of the above? For decades, Muppets cast and creators have mostly dodged the question when asked, but here at Popular Science, we wanted a more scientific answer. So we asked three biologists to take a closer look at Gonzo’s anatomy and tell us what kind of creature he might be.

Their answers took us somewhere we definitely weren’t expecting, all the way back to the age of the dinosaurs. So what is Gonzo, and can science finally solve one of the Muppets’ greatest mysteries?

Welcome to Ask Us Anything from the editors of Popular Science, where we answer your questions about our weird world. From “does candy taste different now?” to “how do airplane toilets work?” No question is too simple or too out there. I’m Sarah Durn, an editor at Popular Science.

Annie Colbert: And hello, I am Popular Science editor-in-chief and huge Muppets fan, Annie Colbert

SD: Here at PopSci, we’re always pondering weirdo questions.

AC: And this week we’re wondering: What animal might Gonzo be? Is he an animal at all?

SD: It’s a very fair question, one the writers of the Muppets have spent over 50 years dodging. In one film, Gonzo even asked to be called a whatever.

AC: Which is pretty classic Gonzo, but as science journalists, “whatever” doesn’t quite hold up under peer review.

SD: Not at all. So we took Gonzo’s anatomy to actual evolutionary biologists and paleontologists to see if they could decode his unique physiology.

AC: Let me guess. They told you he’s just a funny-looking bird?

SD: That’s what you might think. He’s got that down curved beak thing, a floof atop on his head that kinda looks like feathers, and a chicken for a girlfriend.

But when you look at the clues, like his three unfused fingers and fuzzy skin, things get way weirder.

AC: Weirder than a blue guy who eats rubber tires and catches cannonballs?

SD: Well, at least on a similar level of weird, I guess. Some scientists think his traits point tens of millions of years into the past, past modern birds, straight into the age of carnivorous dinosaurs.

AC: Wait, are you telling me that Gonzo might be closer to a T-Rex than a turkey?

SD: Let’s just say Jurassic Park might need a Muppets section.

AC: Hmm. Now, before we try to decode the Muppet fossil record, we wanna know, what questions are nagging you? If there’s something you’ve always wanted to know, submit your questions by clicking the Ask Us link at popsci.com/ask.

Again, that’s popsci.com/ask, and click the Ask Us link.

AC: We’ll be right back after this quick break to find out if science can really classify the greatest daredevil in puppet history.

SD: And stick around to the end, because we’ll be joined by the legendary David Goelz, the original and longtime performer of Gonzo, to hear his take on what sort of life form Gonzo might be.

And we’re back. Now, Annie, before we dive into the mysteries of Muppet evolution, we need to establish your credentials here a bit, because you are far from just a casual fan. You are a certified Muppet expert.

SD: Okay, so how did your Muppet obsession begin?

AC: You know, there’s no start to my love of Muppets.

I grew up in a Muppet house with The Muppet Show and Sesame Street always on. I’ve always identified as a bit of a whimsical weirdo. I dressed up even as Grundgetta, who is Oscar the Grouch’s girlfriend, for Halloween in fourth grade. No one knew who I was, but I will share a photo, so you can judge for yourselves, listeners.

And I would say generally if people know one or two things about me, it’s either that I have strange cats or that I love the Muppets. It’s a very big part of who I am.

SD: I mean, you have your own Muppet wiki page.

AC: I do! It just appeared one day after I did some fun work with Sesame Street, but it is a life highlight to have.

SD: I mean, so casual, so cool. Um, honestly, I think I’m a little intimidated because I am walking into this episode possessing maybe 1% of your Muppet knowledge. I think I saw a couple of the Muppet films when I was growing up.

AC: Don’t worry at all. The Muppets accept all, even the uninitiated.

SD: Well, I’m very happy to be here as an uninitiated Muppet fan, especially because this episode is just so fun and goofy and feels very PopSci.

AC: Yes, absolutely. I love giving scientific thought to some seriously silly questions because, as we know, science is fueled by curiosity.

SD: Of course. All right, so as our Muppet expert, I have to ask, if you had to put a label on Gonzo, what is he?

AC: Hmm. I think I would probably refer back to Muppet canon and say a whatever.

AC: Right. Well, in the 1981 film The Great Muppet Caper, a few of the Muppets get shipped to London in labeled crates. So Kermit’s says “frog,” Fozzie’s says “bear,” and Gonzo’s just says “whatever.”

AC: Very. But the Muppets haven’t always been super consistent with how they define what Gonzo is.

Three years earlier in the 1979 Muppet Movie, Kermit calls Gonzo sort of like a turkey. And then in 1999 in Muppets From Space, Gonzo was briefly labeled as an extraterrestrial.

AC: But for the most part, his species is left pretty ambiguous. It’s kind of become a running joke.

I may not have your Muppet know-how, but I can definitely ask experts some silly Muppet-related questions.

SD: So the first expert we consulted is Darren Naish, a paleontologist who studies extinct vertebrae anatomy, and Naish lines up a bit with Kermit’s turkey theory. He thinks Gonzo is a bird.

AC: A bird? So is he agreeing with Kermit’s turkey comment?

SD: Sort of. He looked at the evidence. Gonzo is fuzzy, so he’s likely warm-blooded. He’s got four limbs, a backbone, no teeth, and that curved beak-looking snout. And if you add all of those together, Naish says he can’t be anything other than a bird.

AC: Okay. I hear the logic, but I’m not fully abandoning my whatever theory just yet.

SD: Fair enough. Well, Naish actually got way more specific than a turkey. He looks at Gonzo’s slender, down-curving snout and sees an ibis, one of those long-billed wading birds.

AC: Okay, but ibises fly, and Gonzo only flies if he’s shot out of a cannon.

SD: Naish actually thought of that. It turns out birds lose flight all the time in evolutionary history. In fact, an extinct Jamaican ibis from about 10,000 years ago lost the ability to fly, and its wing bones actually evolved into heavy club-like weapons that it used to smack rivals in fights.

AC: Cool. They’re just swinging club hands in a brawl.

AC: I mean, honestly, that sounds extremely Gonzo. But not in a violent way. It’d be in a silly way. He’d be like-

SD: Of course, of course. So Naish’s theory is that Gonzo could be a highly derived flightless ibis.

AC: Okay. I kinda love that, but it still feels a little too normal for him.

SD: Well, hold onto your tuft of blue fuzz. Enter our second paleontologist, Thomas Holtz from the University of Maryland, who specializes in carnivorous dinosaurs. And Holtz looked at Gonzo and said, “You’re looking at the wrong geological era. Gonzo is actually way older, Jurassic kind of old.”

SD: A dinosaur. Holtz looked at Gonzo’s hands, and if you look at modern birds, their wing bones are fused together with drastically reduced digits. But Gonzo, Gonzo has three distinct, fully functioning, unfused fingers on each hand.

AC: True. I mean, he does have to hold his stunt props somehow.

SD: Exactly. And Holtz noted that Gonzo’s body is covered in simple down-like fuzz, with just a few complex feathers on his head. According to Holtz, you only see those two specific traits together, three free fingers and simple fuzzy coats, in early carnivorous dinosaurs from a group called Tetanurae.

AC: Tetanurae? What? Okay, who else is in that club?

SD: Oh, just the ancestors of raptors and early tyrannosaurs.

AC: No way. Tyrannosaurus rex? Is Gonzo related to a T-rex?

SD: Maybe. Holtz points out that other Muppets who are clearly birds, like Big Bird or Camilla and her chicken friends, have modern veined feathers and hard, shiny keratin beaks.

Gonzo has neither. So Holtz argues that if Gonzo is in the bird lineage, he split off tens of millions of years before modern feathers or fused wings ever evolved. He’s a living prehistoric relic.

AC: I don’t think Camilla realizes she’s dating an ancient theropod dinosaur, but you know what, honestly, good for her.

SD: Aim high, Camilla. But we had one more scientist weigh in, Michel Milinkovitch, an evolutionary developmental biologist at the University of Geneva, and he said the whole debate hinges on one single question: What is that tuft on Gonzo’s head made of?

SD: Yes. Milinkovitch says it could just be convergent evolution, a mammal that independently evolved a beak-like snout, like the platypus.

AC: My brain is malfunctioning. So he’s either a modified ibis, a fuzzy Jurassic carnivore, or a bizarre egg-laying mammal cousin.

SD: Yes. You got it. Your brain is doing fine.

SD: And to make matters even more confusing, though, Holtz points out the biggest scientific problem of all: Gonzo’s nose isn’t actually a beak at all.

SD: In birds and turtles, the beak is the mouth. It’s the actual jaw bone covered in hard keratin. But for Gonzo, that big purple nose thing is an extension sitting above and in front of his mouth. It doesn’t have the hard shine of keratin, and it doesn’t move like an elephant’s trunk. Holtz says it’s an anatomical structure that is basically unheard of in vertebrate biology.

AC: Leave it to Gonzo to have a face that literally defies anatomy. My whatever theory still holds water.

SD: It really does. And Darren Naish actually had a great philosophical take on this. He pointed out that nobody asks what creature other Muppets like Animal or Elmo are because they don’t have distinct anatomical clues. But Gonzo has just enough real anatomy, feathers, a beak, three fingers, a chicken for a partner, to make our human brains desperate to categorize him. As Naish put it, “Specificity invites scrutiny.”

AC: And the more details you give us, the more obsessed we become with solving the puzzle.

SD: Exactly. So whether he’s an ibis, a dinosaur, or an evolutionary wild card, science still can’t give us a tidy one-word label.

AC: Which means, Sarah, there is only one logical thing left for us to do. We’ve heard what the paleontologists and the developmental biologists have to say, but what does the man behind the Muppet think?

SD: That’s right. Up next, Annie sits down with the one and only David Goelz, the legendary puppeteer who has performed and voiced Gonzo since day one. She asks Dave what he thinks Gonzo really is, how that iconic character was born, and whether he agrees with Team Dinosaur.

AC: Truly a dream come true. That’s right after this quick break.

Welcome back. I am thrilled to welcome Muppet legend Dave Goelz. Dave has been the voice and spirit, I’d say, of Gonzo for 50 years. He also originated a number of other beloved characters, including Uncle Traveling Matt of Fraggle Rock fame, as well as Muppets Zoot, Beauregard, and of course, Dr. Bunsen Honeydew.

Dave Goelz: Well, thank you for having me.

AC: Yes. So we have spent this episode trying to figure out what Gonzo might be in a scientific sense, and since you know him better than anyone, what do you think Gonzo actually is?

DG: Well, I can answer from our particular corner of the field.

When the Muppets started out, they tended to be almost always abstract characters. There was one humanoid in their first series. The series was called Sam and Friends, and Sam looked like a, a person, but everybody else on the show looked like things we’d never seen before. And then when we went on Sesame Street, this is before, before I was there, actually, they went on Sesame Street, they, it stayed with abstract characters, Ernie and Bert, Grover.

Grover is considered a monster. And they stayed with those abstract characters for quite a long time, and then when we did The Muppet Show, all of a sudden we were surprised to see pigs and chickens…

DG: I remember thinking, “This is weird, the Muppets are abstract. Why do we, why do we have a pig?” You know? “Why do, why do we have a chicken?” It was just an interesting transition ’cause that’s when we went more literal with, with species. Getting around to answering your question, I don’t know what Gonzo is. I have no idea. He was something that Jim built for a previous special, as you know, and when it came time to do The Muppet Show, Jim asked me to do this character who was kind of a loser outsider who does stupid acts and thinks they’re high art.

And then he asked for them to pull Gonzo out. Or that, that puppet that wasn’t Gonzo yet.

AC: What were your first impressions when you saw the puppet itself?

DG: Well, I had seen it before, so it wasn’t a surprise, but it was this pathetic-looking little guy, who had very downcast eyes. He was sort of limited, but I just started making a character out of him, and what my interest in him has always been is his character. And iin that one character, I found that it mirrored me. The reason that it did was because Jerry Juhl, who was our head writer and a very wise person and very funny and mischievous person, could see, I guess, that I was new.

I had no business in show business. I had no training. I had no acting training. We just started The Muppet Show, and Jim tossed me in, and I felt very out of place. I just go, “I don’t belong here. What am I doing in this room?” And so Jerry Juhl helped write Gonzo to be appropriate to where I was in life, and that was phase one. He was an outsider. He had a little bit of a baby talk accent…

DG: like a true newbie. And then as time went by, and I’m talking about years, I got more confident, and then one of our writers, Bill Prady, he started writing Gonzo as being very upbeat and enthusiastic. Like, “That is so cool,” you know, and, and just up for anything, and that became phase two of his character, which coincided with me being more comfortable in my new world And then phase three came when Jerry Juhl wanted to include Dickensian prose in the Muppet Christmas Carol film.

He needed that narrative prose in there, but didn’t want to have a narrator, and he had the idea, because we were very close friends, and he’d watched me go through therapy, and he’d watched me deepen and soften and evolve. He had the idea of letting Gonzo speak those lines.

AC: I feel like people have been asking this question since we all met Gonzo. Why do you think people care so much?

DG: Oh, I think I’ve learned a lot about that in the last, I don’t know, 10 years, let’s say. Whenever I appear at a museum or introduce a screening, people come up to me, and so many people come up and say, “Thank you. Gonzo gave me permission to be different.”

DG: He legitimized it. He made it cool. And a lot of these people are on the spectrum, and they are lovely people who have a hard time in life. And it was unintentional on my part. I didn’t know that they were, that Gonzo was having this effect on people, but he did.

And then about four months ago, I, I realized suddenly that, oh, wait a minute, no, no, this was unconscious on my part. I knew I was different. I didn’t belong in show business. I should be on my parents’ couch, you know, watching on the other end.

AC: Yeah, I feel like, I’m sure people have said this to you, you know, I think people think of Kermit as the heart of the Muppets, and they think of Gonzo as kind of the soul of the Muppets, and I think that nebulousness around what he is, of like not really knowing, I think it allows a lot of people, you know, myself included, that you can find a piece of yourself in him.

If you’ve ever felt excluded or weird, because he is not defined, there is lots of room to sort of hold a piece of him as a fan.

DG: Oh, Annie, that’s absolutely true. Absolutely true. He’s been that for people, and I have to say also that the Muppets as a whole are like that, too. They function the same way.

DG: Jim was a lover of characters. He hired characters. He hired all sorts of unusual people and found something for them to do and let them shine. It’s like I didn’t create Gonzo. It was me and the writers and Jim and the workshop. And these qualities exist in every single character, and there’s somebody out there who responds to every single one.

AC: You have a little bit of like an engineering and design background, right?

DG: I do, yeah. I was an industrial designer by training.

AC: Yeah, and I think especially lately there’s this sort of stark line between art and science, but you know, what we see, especially at Popular Science, is we see really amazing innovations can happen when art and science overlap.

So how do you bring a little bit of that engineering mind to playing a Muppet?

DG: A couple of things. First of all, when I first began, I already knew how to build puppets because I was trained as a designer at Art Center College of Design, and the design process was something that my dad inculcated into me, and then ArtCenter set in place.

And the design process that I use is about defining the problem, whether it’s a character, a performance, a glasses case, a typewriter. Whatever it is, it’s very important to know what the problem is, and it’s not always obvious. Listen, the reason I love that approach is that the more you hone in on the problem, the clearer the solution becomes.

AC: One final question. Because we’re Popular Science, I must ask about the Muppets’ preeminent scientist, Dr. Bunsen Honeydew-

AC: whom, of course, you also perform. If Bunsen, or Dr. Honeydew, he earned his degree, won a Nobel Prize, what do you think it would be for?

DG: Well, first of all, the idea is preposterous-

DG: On its face. That’s a great question. If he won a Noble Prize, what would it be for? A Nobel Peace Prize. All he’s done in life is make stupid inventions and hurt his assistant.

DG: So it really is a preposterous notion. I can’t even answer it.

I can’t. It’s just a mind-boggling question. I don’t have any idea how he could possibly be recognized for anything. I will tell you this, that Bunsen was, Bunsen was derived from a lot of scientists that I knew when I was in Silicon Valley. It wasn’t anybody directly, but it was this whole idea of being focused on electrons and being focused on tiny, tiny, very specific things, and losing the big picture.

DG: Yeah. ‘Cause it’s interesting you know, a scientist might be way deep into making a laser interferometer, and the science of it would be so riveting. And then my job was to come along and say, “Okay, what does it look like? How do you use it?” So I was, like, the user end of this whole deal. And, and so as a generalist, I could view the science world and the engineering world, and, uh, poke a little fun at it.

AC: Absolutely. Science is fun. We like to remind people.

AC: I will take off my journalist hat just for a second and say thank you so much for doing the podcast, but also just thank you so much for Gonzo. What you said about people who have maybe been called different or weird, it definitely resonates with me.

I’ve loved the Muppets my entire life, and being called weird my whole life is such a compliment because there’s so much joy and whimsy in the weirdos of Muppets, and Gonzo is such the epitome of that, that I thank you so much, Dave, for joining us today.

SD: Oh my gosh, was your inner Muppet heart exploding while talking to Dave? Yes. He seemed so wonderful.

AC: Yeah, he is just an absolute gem of a human. I did not even try to keep my fandom in check ’cause he’s a legend, and he’s genuinely meant so much to me as a Muppet fan.

SD: He’s the best. Oh my God. So after hearing from Dave and all of our biologists where do you, Muppet expert, officially land on the taxonomy of a Gonzo?

AC: Okay, I started the episode firmly on team whatever, but now I kinda love the idea that Camilla is casually dating a prehistoric dinosaur. But I also like the idea that Gonzo doesn’t have to be defined. He can be something different for everyone, like, whatever they need him to be.

SD: But the dinosaur theory does make his cannonball catching stunt seem a lot more on brand for a T-Rex relative.

And if you like our show, leave a rating and a review.

SD: Which Muppet do you want scientists to analyze next? Tell us in the comments. Please. Our producer is Alan Haburchak. This week’s episode was based on an article written for Popular Science by Niranjana Rajalakshmi, and a massive thank you to the legendary Dave Goelz for joining us.

AC: Thank you, team. Thank you, Dave, and thanks all you Muppets for listening.

SD: And one more time, if you want something you’ve always wondered about explained on a future episode, go to popsci.com/ask and click the Ask Us link. Until next time, stay weird wherever you are, and keep the questions coming.

#4682. Does Terrorism Really Bring People Together?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

On a Sunday afternoon in November 2022, a bomb exploded on Istiklal Avenue, one of the busiest streets in Istanbul. Six people were killed, and 81 were injured.

After an attack like this, we tend to tell a hopeful story. Tragedy brings people together. People line up to give blood, flags appear on balconies, and for a while strangers treat each other like neighbors.

By chance, my colleagues and I were in a position to test it.

A month before the bombing, we had surveyed 620 adults in Türkiye for an unrelated project. Almost nine in 10 lived in Istanbul. They answered questions about their moral values and made two decisions with money.

When the bomb went off, we realized we had something rare: a record of how people in the city thought and behaved just before a terrorist attack. Researchers often arrive only after the event or compare one group of people before it with a different group after it.

So we registered our predictions in advance and, about two and a half months after the attack, invited the same people back. In the end, 222 took part a second time.

The results have just been published in Social Psychological and Personality Science (Velioglu et al., 2026). The project began as the master’s thesis of Ilayda Velioglu, now a PhD candidate in my lab, and was funded by the European Research Council.

To measure values, we used a questionnaire based on moral foundations theory (Atari et al., 2023). It separates two families of moral concern.

One is about protecting individuals: caring for those who suffer and treating people equally. The other is about holding a group together: loyalty, respect for authority, and sanctity. Researchers call this second family “binding” values.

After the bombing, binding values went up. The rise was small, from 3.98 to 4.08 on a five-point scale, and it did not depend on people’s political views.

The money decisions pointed the other way.

In the first, each person received 100 Turkish liras, about $5.50 at the time, and could give any part of it to an anonymous stranger. Before the bombing, people gave about 36 liras on average. After it, they gave about 29.

In the second, people could put any part of 100 liras into a group fund. Whatever went in was doubled and shared equally among all members. The group does best when everyone contributes, but each person does best by keeping their own money.

Here we added an experiment. Half of the returning participants read a short description of the bombing and answered questions about how threatened they felt before making their choices. The other half made their choices first.

Those who were reminded of the attack put in less than they had before, about 40 liras compared with 46. Those who were not reminded put in about as much as before.

These were not imaginary choices. In each game, one participant picked by lottery was paid according to the decisions actually made.

One well-known idea is that threat makes liberals think more like conservatives (Nail et al., 2009). After the 2005 London bombings, a British study found that liberals’ moral views moved toward those of conservatives (Van de Vyver et al., 2016).

We expected the same and did not find it. The rise in binding values was similar on the left and the right.

The other family of values, care and equality, did not change on average. But the average hid a difference. People further to the right valued them less after the bombing, while those on the left showed little change. Being reminded of the attack made no difference here.

This was the opposite of what we predicted, so I treat it as a lead for future studies.

The setting may explain part of it. In an earlier study of ours, young voters on both the left and the right in Türkiye endorsed binding values to a considerable degree (Yilmaz et al., 2016). Theories built on American and British samples may not apply everywhere.

After the September 11 attacks, researchers recorded a jump in volunteering in the United States (Penner et al., 2005). But much of the evidence for generosity after attacks comes from what people say they gave or plan to give, and such reports can run high (Steinberg & Rooney, 2005). Our participants had to give up money.

The kind of threat may matter as well. People tend to donate less to victims of disasters caused by humans than to victims of natural ones (Zagefka et al., 2011).

The stranger in our games was someone participants knew nothing about.

As we put it in the paper, threats “may narrow individuals’ moral and social focus.” People may hold tighter to those they know and share less with those they do not. We did not test giving to family or neighbors, so this remains a guess.

The limits are real. This is one attack in one country, and the changes were small.

A before-and-after comparison cannot prove that the bombing caused them, because other things also changed in Türkiye over those months. Only about a third of the eligible participants returned, and the earthquake of February 6, 2023, forced us to stop collecting data early.

The strongest evidence is the reminder experiment, because there, chance alone decided who was reminded.

Still, after the attack, the same people said loyalty and authority mattered more, and they gave less to a stranger.

Feeling united and acting generously are different things. So the next time an attack is followed by talk of unity, ask two questions. United with whom? And does it show in what people do, or only in what they say?

Atari, M., Haidt, J., Graham, J., Koleva, S., Stevens, S. T., & Dehghani, M. (2023). Morality beyond the WEIRD: How the nomological network of morality varies across cultures. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 125(5), 1157–1188. https://doi.org/10.1037/pspp0000470

Nail, P. R., McGregor, I. A., Drinkwater, A. E., Steele, G. M., & Thompson, A. W. (2009). Threat causes liberals to think like conservatives. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 45(4), 901–907. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jesp.2009.04.013

Penner, L. A., Brannick, M. T., Webb, S. L., & Connell, P. W. (2005). Effects on volunteering of the September 11, 2001, attacks: An archival analysis. Journal of Applied Social Psychology, 35(7), 1333–1360. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1559-1816.2005.tb02173.x

Steinberg, K. S., & Rooney, P. (2005). America gives: A survey of Americans’ generosity after September 11. Nonprofit and Voluntary Sector Quarterly, 34(1), 110–135. https://doi.org/10.1177/0899764004269738

Van de Vyver, J., Houston, D. M., Abrams, D., & Vasiljevic, M. (2016). Boosting belligerence: How the July 7, 2005, London bombings affected liberals’ moral foundations and prejudice. Psychological Science, 27(2), 169–177. https://doi.org/10.1177/0956797615615584

Velioglu, I., Yilmaz, O., Dogruyol, B., Isler, O., & Gächter, S. (2026). Terrorism frays morality: The effects of the 2022 Istanbul bombing on moral foundations, generosity, and cooperation. Social Psychological and Personality Science. Advance online publication. https://doi.org/10.1177/19485506261503120

Yilmaz, O., Saribay, S. A., Bahçekapili, H. G., & Harma, M. (2016). Political orientations and moral foundations of young Turkish voters. Turkish Studies, 17(4), 544–566. https://doi.org/10.1080/14683849.2016.1221312

Zagefka, H., Noor, M., Brown, R., de Moura, G. R., & Hopthrow, T. (2011). Donating to disaster victims: Responses to natural and humanly caused events. European Journal of Social Psychology, 41(3), 353–363. https://doi.org/10.1002/ejsp.781

#4681. Volkswagen is delaying another EV based on the SSP

After delaying development of the long-awaited electric Golf, Volkswagen is delaying another EV based on its SSP platform.

As it scrambles to cut costs, Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer revealed in an internal memo at the end of October that development of the all-electric Golf is being delayed at its Wolfsburg plant in Germany.

The news comes after the VW Group posted an operating loss of €5.9 billion ($6.5 billion) in the third quarter, its largest quarterly loss since the infamous Dieselgate scandal in 2015.

“We simply can’t afford this work right now,” Schäfer said in the memo reviewed by Reuters. The Wolfsburg plant, AKA the “heart of the VW brand,” is about €300 million ($334.5 million) short of its cost-cutting targets, the memo said.

Volkswagen initially planned to launch the Golf EV in 2028, but Schäfer announced earlier this year that the long-awaited electric car was delayed until closer to 2030.

Schäfer suggested the delay was because the SSP (Scalable Systems Platform), which is being developed through its partnership with Rivian, was taking longer than expected, again due to costs.

According to Autocar, Volkswagen is now delaying the Audi A4 E-tron as well, another vehicle that was initially planned to be among the first based on the SSP platform.

Production of the electric A4 is being pushed back until at least 2029, a year later than originally planned. While the delay is disappointing for Audi fans (including myself) still waiting for an electric A4, it also puts Audi behind rival luxury brands in the mid-size sedan segment.

BMW has the new i3, and Mercedes-Benz has the C-Class EV, both of which feature major improvements in range, charging, and efficiency over their previous-generation EVs.

Volkswagen said in 2023 that the 800V SSP will serve as a “single future backbone with integrated electric and electronics architecture,” claiming that more than 40 million models were expected to be built on it.

The company also said investment and R&D costs were expected to be reduced by about 30% compared to the current MEB platform, enabling most models “to achieve the same margin compared to their conventionally powered counterparts.”

Volkswagen’s software struggles started in its internal division, Cariad, leading to delays, missed targets, and budget overruns.

To fix it, VW turned to Rivian, forming a joint venture to develop its next-gen software-defined vehicle (SDV) electrical architecture.

In March, VW said several test vehicles, including the ID.EVERY1, Audi, and Scout with the SDV architecture underwent “comprehensive evaluation,” and successfully validated over-the-air (OTA) functionality.

Being cash efficient is good, but delays to the next-gen platform that will keep you competitive with rival brands seem like a problem.

However, the Audi A4 E-tron delay is not entirely about software. The Autocar report claims Audi demanded significant changes to the SSP platform for the A4 E-tron so it more closely matched the current gas version.

Audi reportedly wanted individual footwells for front and rear passengers, which would require repositioning the battery.

The luxury brand also reportedly asked for a 48V electrical system instead of the traditional 12V setup initially planned.

While development of the Golf EV is on hold, VW’s works council said the pause will not delay its launch, promising to make up for lost time. It’s still expected to launch in 2030. The Audi A4 E-tron is now expected to arrive around 2029.

#4680. Grad student finds New Mexico’s first Canada lynx in 25 years

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 13, 2026 11:00 AM EST

In June, New Mexico State University graduate student William Grooms was using motion-sensing cameras to investigate wildlife in Carson National Forest in northern New Mexico. And when he looked through his first images, he spotted something flabbergasting.

His cameras had captured a series of photographs of a Canada lynx (Lynx canadensis)—a wild cat that hasn’t been documented in the state for around 25 years. But Grooms had to make sure it wasn’t actually a bobcat (Lynx rufus), which is a similar-looking species.

“It caught my eye because the cat in the image had the characteristic ear tufts and facial ruff [of bobcats], but it was lacking the black spots that are typical of bobcats,” Grooms, who is studying in the department of Fish, Wildlife and Conservation Ecology, tells Popular Science. “We also have a good image of the tail, which on lynx has a solid black tip compared to a bobcat whose tail has white on the underside, so my confidence grew.”

He and his team also showed the image to other researchers for confirmation. Ultimately, there’s no doubt about the fact that the big cat slinking through the dark was indeed a Canada lynx. The species lives in dense boreal and subalpine forests and woodlands throughout much of Canada and Alaska. They have long legs, grayish or yellowish-brown coats, and wide fur-lined paws.

Their main prey are snowshoe hares (Lepus americanus), which they follow into the forest understory—the ground-level area of downed trees and dense vegetation beneath which the hares hide and live. The problem is that these kinds of habitats are fire hazards. Recent forest fire mitigation efforts include decreasing dangerous fuel loads via thinning, prescribed burning, or timber harvesting.

“While these tactics reduce the risk of severe fires, they also remove important habitat features,” Grooms explains. “Our objective is to provide managers with practical, science-based advice regarding what effects fuel reduction treatments and timber harvesting have on wildlife in the Southern Rocky Mountains so that they can make well-informed decisions as they go about their task of managing our nation’s forests.”

Simply knowing that at least one Canada lynx was in the area provides more data for this mission.

#4678. Transformation Doesn't Have to Be Hard

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 22, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

People struggle with life's inevitable challenges, traumas large and small, and the chaos of our times everywhere. Throughout Gina Vild’s career, most recently as an associate dean at Harvard Medical School, she has been fascinated by what psychology and neuroscience tell us about our capacity to thrive in the face of adversity. She has also watched people confront profound hardship, heal over time, and thrive. Vild has navigated her own adversity of loss early in life and profound betrayal. She shows this in her recent book, Buoyant.

GV: No one escapes life’s inevitable losses, disappointments, and unexpected turns. When confronted with adversity, some people rail against the darkness while others think, "Barn's burned down, now I can see the moon?” Buoyant people cultivate a mindset that enables them to adapt, heal, and grow. Some pillars of resilience:

LM: If adversity is unavoidable, how do we become who we were?

GV: That may not happen. By moving through the difficulties life hurls and mining them for lessons, we often emerge changed and wiser. We are butterflies. Only by leaving the comfort of the chrysalis can it spread its wings and fly. We can discover our most beautiful lives by embracing transformation and remaining open to all possibilities.

LM: If we can't restore an old life, how do we build a new one?

GV: Each person navigates their pain differently; no single roadmap or certainty will get us there, but common threads exist.

Buoyant people know they have a choice. They recognize they cannot control what happens to them, but they can choose how they will respond. They can remain trapped in the past and carry sorrow like a heavy backpack. Or choose to look forward, embrace hope as a discipline, take purposeful action, manage unruly emotions, and reach for connection.

Buoyant people accept and grieve what is forever lost. Grief is love’s necessary counterpoint. When we choose to love deeply, we are accepting the possibility of profound sorrow. When we can see grief as a healing balm, we pay tribute not only to what we have lost, but to the immeasurable gift of having loved deeply.

Buoyant people find the courage to embrace the unfamiliar and accept the risk of not knowing where the path will lead. Detours and zigzags litter the path, but also opportunities to discover unimaginable possibilities. The Journal of Traumatic Stress reports that reaching for new possibilities is a hallmark of posttraumatic growth. As the poet John O'Donohue reminds us: “Awaken your spirit to adventure. Hold nothing back, learn to find ease in risk.”

LM: How do we keep the past from controlling our future?

GV: We cannot change the past, but we can stop letting it replay in a mind loop. Our thoughts hold extraordinary power over every aspect of our lives, and learning to manage them can change life.

Even a fleeting thought can spark a decision, a habit, or a change in direction. When our thoughts hold us back, one of the most empowering things we can do is learn to change the channel. With practice, we can teach ourselves to observe the thoughts whispering in our ear and catch them before they land. We see destructive thought loops and flip the script. We may not control which thoughts arise, but we can choose which ones deserve attention.

GV: When hardship strikes, it’s like a single, overwhelming black dot on the screen of our life. It dominates our field of vision, blotting out all else. To ease the sorrow and regain perspective, pull back, widen the aperture, and let the light in. That light comes from gratitude. Gratitude is not a platitude; it's a catalyst for mental toughness, physical health, and greater happiness.

LM: How do we become present in life, and not just get through it?

GV: Mindfulness, the practice of renewing our minds and tending to our bodies, returns us to who we are at our essence. By stripping away worry, fear, obligation, and distraction, mindfulness anchors us in the present moment, enhancing mental clarity and emotional stability. This can come through guided meditation, journaling, yoga, knitting, music, time in nature, or enjoying a pet. When we are fully present, we don't just move through our days.

LM: How do we release resentment without excusing wrongdoing?

GV: Through forgiveness, we release resentment over a past hurt and permit ourselves to move from pain to a mindset where we can flourish. We can choose peace and healing over bitterness and blame. An international study in BMJ Public Health underscores the restorative power of forgiveness; practicing it can ease depression and anxiety. Yet some struggle with forgiveness, equating it with absolution. But forgiveness doesn’t condone past harm.

Nelson Mandela understood this. After 27 years in prison, he walked toward the gate upon his release and had a revelation: Liberation required the release of bitterness and hatred. If he carried them through the prison gates, he would still be in prison.

LM: Some people are strong in gratitude and community but struggle with forgiveness or acceptance. How do we ameliorate this?

GV: We can cultivate qualities that don't come easily. Acceptance and forgiveness become a gift. These are three essential components:

Accept that storms will blow through your life. Many of these unwelcome events are beyond your control.

Accept that you are not exempt from pain. Once we accept that suffering is part of the human experience, and that none of us is immune, we are comforted by seeing suffering as a bond that unites all of humanity.

Accept that healing takes time. You cannot rush the process. Allow all your emotions; take time to grieve. Grief needs time to do its healing work.

LM: How do we take responsibility for our own healing?

GV: We cannot control the past, but we can shape the future. We can strengthen resilience. Decades of research, including a BMJ Open review, confirms that resilience can be bolstered in response to adverse events, setbacks, and disappointments. As the Buddha reminds us, “Every life has a measure of sorrow, and sometimes this is what awakens us.” We can choose this awakening by using proven practices, seeking support, and taking purposeful steps toward healing. In doing so, we mine our sadness for wisdom and discover strengths we never knew we possessed.

Buoyant: The Art and Science of a Resilient Life, by Gina Vild. Broadleaf Books.‎ December 1, 2026.

#4677. Ghosts don’t scare German shepherds

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 13, 2026 12:00 PM EST

The German shepherd was originally bred to do exactly what their name implies, but a lot has changed since Max von Stephanitz introduced the breed in 1899. Today, the German shepherd is one of the world’s most recognizable and popular dogs, largely due to their intelligence, trainability, and companionship. You’re just as likely to spot one of them at an airport sniffing for contraband as you are at a kennel club competition.

But a good “work” German shepherd and a good show dog require two very different sets of traits. According to researchers at Sweden’s Uppsala University, these specific qualities are so pronounced that they’re even visible at the genetic level. What’s more, many of these genes can also be seen in humans.

“It’s interesting that we can now see that this selective breeding has indeed led to differences between working dogs and show dogs among German shepherds—differences that can be seen at both the behavioral and genetic levels,” Uppsala University genomics researcher Kerstin Lindblad-Toh explained in a recent profile.

Lindblad-Toh and her colleagues laid out their findings in a study recently published in the journal Animal Genetics. To assess the iconic breed, the team reviewed a massive dataset of 23,000 German shepherds who previously participated in a standardized behavioral test known as the Dog Mentality Assessment (DMA). During the DMA, canines are exposed to a range of situations, such as meeting strangers, play time, and even encountering imposing, ghostly figures. The team discovered that while German shepherds often scored higher for traits like neuroticism and shyness, the breed’s working dogs generally exhibited more curiosity, less fear, and a willingness to socialize with people.

“Breeders of working dogs have selected and bred the ones that really enjoy working; it’s a bit like a game for them,” said Lindblad-Toh.

From there, the researchers gathered blood samples and mapped the genomes of 373 German shepherds who previously took the DMA. Some of these behavioral divergences were so stark that the study’s authors could pinpoint them in the dogs’ genetics.

“We could then see that there were areas in the genome where differences could be seen in the dogs depending on how curious or playful they were, for example,” Lindblad-Toh said. “That meant that we were able to identify some of the genes in working dogs that are linked to curiosity and playfulness.”

In some instances, the same genes influencing German shepherd personalities are also tied to the same behaviors in humans. This means it may be possible to further explore human psychology with the aid of our best animal friends. Although Lindblad-Toh cautioned that their study is “just a first step” along this path, they hope to learn more about specific breed genetic traits and their overlap with owners.

“We now have an example of how we might also acquire more knowledge about different behaviors in people with [the] help of dogs in the longterm,” she said.

#4676. BYD’s new flagship Tang SUV starts at about $34,000 with two enormous screens

BYD opened pre-orders for the third-generation Tang starting at about $34,000 in China. This five-seat flagship SUV packs more than you’d expect for the money, with two massive 30-inch-plus screens inside and up to 850 km (528 miles) of CLTC range.

The third-generation Tang joins the Great Tang, or Da Tang, as it’s called in China in BYD’s expanding flagship SUV lineup.

We knew it was coming soon after the new model appeared in a regulatory filing in China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) last month.

BYD announced on Friday that pre-orders for the third-gen Tang are officially open, starting at 225,000 yuan, which is around $34,000.

The “large five-seat flagship SUV,” as BYD calls it, is available in three variants, priced from 225,000 yuan ($34,000), 240,000 yuan ($36,000), and 260,000 yuan ($39,000) with rear- and all-wheel-drive variants.

The two lower-priced variants are both RWD, offering a CLTC range of up to 850 km (528 miles), while the top-spec dual-motor AWD version has up to 770 km (478 miles).

All versions use BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging tech, enabling the battery to be charged from 10% to 80% in five minutes, or nine minutes to go from 10% to 97%.

Inside, the five-seat SUV packs a surprising amount of tech and premium extras for the price. The setup features two massive screens: a 35.4″ integrated display and another 30″ panoramic theater screen.

Unlike its predessor, which offered five and six-seat configurations, the third-gen Tang will only be offered as a five-seater.

The five-seat setup opens up interior space for passengers and the third-gen Tang has the largest front trunk (frunk) in its class at 205L, BYD said.

Like many of its new flagship vehicles, the third-gen Tang is equipped with BYD’s latest tech, including its God’s Eye B driver-assistance system and Disus-A dual-chamber intelligent air suspension body control system.

Other added features include a 22-speaker Dynaudio sound system, intelligent electric all‑wheel drive, a high-speed tire blowout stability system, and its iTAC intelligent torque control system.

Lu Tian, the general manager of BYD’s Dynasty division said third-gen Tang vehicles have arrived at dealerships nationwide.

Why mention "two enormous screens" like they are some markers of a more premium vehicle or represent some value? We don't measure the utility of cars by screen real estate per dollar. It's the other part of the utility that matter: range, driving dynamics, road trip convenience, fit/finish/materials/insulation. Personally, I don't think "enormous screens" are going to age well as an automotive trend.

The Great Tang received over 150,000 preorders by the time it launched in mid-June, a record for a single BYD model.

Since its official launch, the larger Great Tang (Da Tang) has sold more than 10,000 units for four straight months now.

The Great Tang is on sale in China in pure electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains. The cheapest EV variant starts at 239,900 yuan ($35,500) a CLTC driving range of 800 km (497 miles). Starting at just 269,900 yuan ($40,000), the Flagship EV version uses a bigger (130.15 kWh) battery, offering a CLTC range of up to 590 miles (950 km).

Will BYD’s smaller five-seat SUV draw the same demand? Let us know your thoughts in the comments below.

#4675. Adventurous baby black bear wins 2026 Courageous Cub Award

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 13, 2026 1:09 PM EST

One little bear cub in Southeastern Alaska’s Tongass National Forest is a true model of bravery. The park’s rangers have awarded the unnamed black bear (Ursus americanus) cub with the 2026 Courageous Cub award for persevering when he got himself in a little pickle this summer. The cub belongs to a forgetful mother bear named Dory, who had two cubs this season.

“This little cub of Dory’s went on a big adventure. He got lost, ran down the trail a half mile and approached visitors as if to ask, ‘Are you my mommy?’ Then got scared and ran off in the wrong direction,” the Tongass rangers write. “Hours later he came running back up the trail sniffing out where mama was.”

Black bears like this family have a very keen sense of smell. It is debated just how far away they can smell, but it is at least two miles and could be up to 20. Fortunately, the cub was able to use some of that sniffing power to find both Dory and his other sibling.

The rangers at Tongass National Forest are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States. It covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau, and includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. This makes the creek a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, at least 39 bears feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Similar to their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their behavior.

#4674. How to Deal With People Who Always Excuse Their Bad Behavior

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 21, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

You’ve met them; I’ve met them: folks who seem always critical or controlling, forgetful or unreliable, and often good at apologizing later. But the apology often ends with a comment like, “I guess it’s just the way I am; I’ve been this way my whole life.” Or, “Because I’ve been doing _____ for so long, I guess my brain is wired to think in terms of ___.” Or, “Because I struggle with—ADHD, depression, anxiety, etc.—I can’t always do _____—e.g., not be late or follow through.”

You want to be sympathetic and understanding, but over time, it all gets old. In your heart of hearts, it starts to feel like a default excuse—their way of dismissing your feelings, of not considering or caring about you, and of leaving you not only frustrated but, at times, even emotionally manipulated.

What’s going on? Why do some people lean on personality weaknesses or mental health diagnoses to explain or excuse what is often simply bad behavior? Here are five common sources:

Your father-in-law always seems critical of you, but in his mind, he is just expressing his opinion, making conversation, or even being helpful by offering suggestions. Pointing out that you feel criticized doesn’t help—he either thinks you’re being too sensitive or rationalizes it by blaming his ingrained habits: Because I’ve been supervising people my whole life, I guess I’m just wired to see the negative.

For some, it’s understandable to be exhausted from trying to manage their depression, anxiety, ADHD, trauma reactions, etc. They've been through dozens of treatments, dozens of drugs that make minimal change at best, but no real relief. They are left feeling that this is what they have to deal with and, often, that they're sorry it affects you as well.

This takes resignation to a higher level, where their struggles have solidified into their overall self-concept: I’m not just a person who struggles with high anxiety, but I am an anxious person, or You don’t understand—I have ______. Sometimes these folks can, understandably, seem overly assertive and rigid, or, once they've informed you, expect you to be automatically accepting and accommodating. If you are not, they can quickly get upset.

Sorry I can’t come into work today, show up for the party, finish my work assignment, or so on because I’m having a flare, I forgot to take my meds, or my _________ is really bad. This goes from explanation to manipulation because they are lying, and their motive is clear: to use their real condition to get what they want. This is often a characterological problem where they lack empathy and use people as tools for their own ends.

So how should you respond in these situations? At a basic level, it’s about shaping a two-sided relationship where you can only control your side. Here are some suggestions.

If your father-in-law keeps brushing off your comments about his criticism, even though you’ve gently explained how it affects you, it’s time to drill down: Ben, I know your comments come from good intentions, and you probably think I’m being overly sensitive, but I don’t understand how, if you care about me—and I believe you do—you don’t make an effort to stop doing what feels hurtful to me.

One obvious path is to have a conversation about that—the giving up—not as a therapist or as someone trying to fix them, but simply as someone who cares about them and wants to understand why they are so discouraged. Your deeper understanding can help you feel less frustrated and more accepting, and the conversation may help them be more sensitive to you.

Time to set boundaries. If you have the clout, call them out on their behavior—require a doctor’s note when they are out sick, or hold them to deadlines at work. If the relationship is more peer-to-peer, do what you need to stop feeling repeatedly taken advantage of: Speak up and tell them how you feel, but more importantly, stop making excuses for them, stop doing the heavy lifting in the relationship, and maybe end it.

Whether it's your dismissive father-in-law, your overly assertive or discouraged friend, or your manipulative employee, they may react negatively to your response, whatever it may be. This is about repairing communication. Here, you work on your side of the relationship by acknowledging their feelings and clarifying what you were trying to convey, without responding in kind or feeling the need to back down. Be sensitive and calm, yet assertive.

Relationships are no longer healthy when they feel out of balance—when you’re not getting enough back for what you give, when you feel used, abused, or simply dismissed. Step back, assess the relationship climate, and advocate for yourself to get what you need.

Is it time to stop making excuses for them and accepting what you get?

Taibbi, R. (2019). Boot camp therapy: Action-oriented approaches to anxiety, anger & depression. New York: Norton.

#4673. Volkswagen may have just hinted at the name of its next affordable EV

Volkswagen is getting ready to launch a new electric car starting at about €20,000 ($22,000) in 2027, and it looks like the entry-level EV may no longer be nameless. A newly filed trademark could have just given away what VW plans to call it.

The new entry-level EV is “the last piece of the puzzle,” Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer said last March after unveiling the ID. EVERY1 concept car.

Volkswagen said the production version will launch in 2027 with a starting price of around €20,000 ($22,000).

The new model will sit below the ID. Polo in Volkswagen’s Electric Urban Car Family, a lineup of compact, affordable electric cars.

Volkswagen’s current entry-level EV lineup includes the ID. Polo, ID. Cross, the Cupra Raval, and Skoda Epiq, all based on its new MEB+ platform.

After launching the lower-priced standard versions of the ID. Polo and ID. Cross recently, starting at €24,995 and €27,995, respectively, Volkswagen is preparing to launch an even smaller, more affordable EV next year.

A recent trademark filing with the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO) and the German DPMA may have just revealed the name of VW’s upcoming €20,000 EV.

Volkswagen filed a trademark application for the name ID. UP on October 22, 2026, with the EUIPO and DPMA, suggesting this will be the name of the upcoming electric car in 2027.

The trademark follows previous reports that VW planned to revive the former Up! name as part of its shift away from its previous numerical naming scheme (ID.3, ID.4, ID.5, etc.).

Volkswagen has kept most details a secret thus far. Like the ID. Polo, the first to go on sale with an established VW nameplate, the ID. UP is expected to use the same 37 kWh LFP battery to reduce costs.

The VW ID. Polo with the 37 kWh battery offers a WLTP range of up to 334 km (207 miles), so the smaller ID. UP will likely provide around the same, if not slightly more.

Volkswagen said it will offer at least 250 km (155 miles) of range. It will also use a new 70 kW (94 hp) electric motor, enabling a top speed of 130 km/h (80 mph).

The production version of the ID. EVERY1, expected to arrive as the ID. UP, will be one of nine new models VW plans to launch by 2027.

Volkswagen previously said the entry-level EV will be 3,880 mm long, which would position it between the former Up! (3,600 mm) and the ID. Polo (4,053 mm). Despite its compact size, VW said the electric city car will seat four passengers and offer a luggage compartment volume of 305 liters.

The VW Group’s new Electric Urban Car Family is off to a strong start, securing nearly 150,000 orders after series production began in June.

All models within the family are built on the MEB+ platform with a FWD powertrain, and share more than 80% of the components and tech.

Volkswagen said the production version of the ID. EVERY1 will be among the first vehicles based on its zonal, software-defined vehicle (SDV) architecture, which it is developing through its joint venture with Rivian.

Ah, finally a car in the upper range of being meaningful and sensible.

If someone needs more, then those are obviously special needs people. Being like can't enter and exit such a sensible car. Or like having to move the 15 horses of their 5 daughters. Or being a fieldworker driving a gazillion miles every day. Or requiring a lot of attention from lesser beings.

In March, the Rivian and Volkswagen Group Technologies (RV Tech) joint venture tested the new SDV architecture on the ID. EVERY1, alongside Audi and Scout reference vehicles, validating over-the-air (OTA) capabilities.

The new architecture will enable “highly automated driving features” and “advanced infotainment solutions,” with continuous OTA updates.

While VW said it will deploy the SDV architecture in “electric vehicles across markets in the Western Hemisphere,” the entry-level EV is not expected to reach the States.

Volkswagen is, however, preparing to launch the ID. Tiguan, which will launch in 2027 as the successor to the ID.4 (and ID.5 in Europe).

#4672. Divers release first footage of SS ‘United States’ after intentional sinking

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 13, 2026 2:00 PM EST

It took a few hours longer than expected, but the SS United States now rests at the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico. The nearly 1,000-foot-long ocean liner sank off the coast of Pensacola, Florida, to a depth of about 190 feet on November 11, where it is now officially the world’s largest artificial reef. In the years ahead, biologists and conservationists will monitor the vessel’s remains as numerous marine species slowly convert the ship into their own home.

Ahead of the next phase in the United States’ recycled life, divers from the RV Explorer swam to document the vessel’s location and post-scuttling condition. On November 13, the team released a brief video of their successful excursion. Interestingly, the footage shows the ship is resting upright on the ocean floor despite initially sinking on its side.

“It was just epic,” diver Rustin Cassway told a local Philadelphia news outlet. “It was very cleaned up. I mean, you could see people really took their time to clean it really nicely.”

The project marks the first time ecologists will be able to monitor a shipwreck’s transformation in real-time. Researchers now plan to conduct annual visits to the SS United States to chart not only the artificial reef’s progress, but how the ship’s materials may affect the surrounding ocean conditions.

In its heyday, the SS United States was the world’s fastest ocean liner. Larger than the RMS Titanic, she was the most powerful, advanced, and modern passenger liner when she first took to the ocean in 1952. In addition to the 1,700 passengers, 7,935 quarts of ice cream and 500 pounds of caviar were also on board. During that maiden voyage (July 3-7, 1952), she broke the transatlantic speed record held by the RMS Queen Mary by over 10 hours. The United States made the crossing from the United Kingdom to New York in three days, 10 hours, and 40 minutes at an average speed of 40.96 mph.

She was designed by naval architect William Francis Gibbs (August 24, 1886 – September 6, 1967), and was built to be converted into a troopship if the United States Navy needed during a time of war. But she never was called into military service. Instead, the United States transported immigrants and celebrities, including future President and First Lady John and Jacqueline Kennedy, actors Grace Kelly, Gary Cooper, and Marilyn Monroe, artist Salvador Dali, and musicians Duke Ellington and Irving Berlin. Walt Disney even filmed parts of the 1962 comedy Bon Voyage aboard the ship.

An engineering marvel, some of the key design features were in the rudder, radar mast, and propellers.

The rudder was designed for good maneuverability at high speeds. The Titanic’s relatively small rudder was one factor behind the ship’s collision with an iceberg and tragic sinking in 1912.

The SS United States had the latest radar equipment, which allowed the crew to see the locations of  other ships and objects in the ocean despite the weather. It was among the first ocean liners to use radar, which was located at one of the highest points on the ship, so in addition to her radar “eyes,” a lookout could be stationed there to warn the captain of any danger in the ship’s path.

Considered a top-secret design, the ship had four propellers—two with four blades and two with five. According to the SS United States Conservancy, this configuration was tested and selected for its superior hydrodynamic performance. The propeller design was overseen by a pioneering Gibbs & Cox engineer named Elaine Kaplan.

Ocean liners became a less attractive option once air travel became quicker and less expensive. The SS United States ceased operations in 1969, and stayed in drydock in several cities before becoming the world’s largest artificial reef.

#4671. Life in Isolation: Are We Living in a Human Zoo?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 22, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader

In Stolen Focus, Johann Hari explores the distress of captive animals through veterinary behaviorist Nicholas Dodman's description of "frustrated biological objectives": innate needs that remain active even when circumstances prevent their expression. Zoochosis describes abnormal behaviors observed in captive animals, including compulsive self-directed activity.

Let’s consider if zoochosis could apply to human beings too: could some of our depression and anxiety be less about defective individuals and more about the increasingly unnatural environments we live in? We recognize something is wrong when a tiger paces endlessly in a concrete enclosure. Yet when human beings experience restlessness, alienation, depression, or anxiety, we are remarkably quick to diagnose them. “I don’t know who discovered water but I doubt it was a fish,” said Marshall McLuhan. Maybe it’s the water that surrounds us that’s toxic and not something inside of us?

Remote work, online shopping, food delivery, streaming entertainment, and virtual socializing have become increasingly normal since the pandemic. Many of these things are genuinely convenient and some have improved people's quality of life. But maybe our frictionless lives are not necessarily an upgrade to the human experience? Maybe we thrive when we have little victories like trips to the store, restaurants, gyms and other third spaces where we interact with others?

We work on one screen, order necessities through another, socialize through messages, exercise in front of a monitor, and unwind by scrolling through videos of other people living lives that appear to be more interesting and exciting than our own. We can spend days on end interacting with two-dimensional representations of the world without actually being face-to-face with other people. Ever heard of pheromones?

We accumulate hundreds of online acquaintances without experiencing the vulnerability and authenticity that we need and crave. We communicate constantly while remaining profoundly lonely.

Humans evolved to move through complex physical terrains, not sit on couches with laptops on our laps. We need touching, exploring, smelling, creating, cooperating, taking risks, and belonging to communities in three dimensions, not two.

And being constantly available is not our friend. Neither is excessive optimization nor compulsive productivity. Having no time for friends, family, or contemplation should be seen as failure. We can no longer simply take a walk; we need to track our steps, monitor our heart rates, and demonstrate that we have accomplished something in contrast to “just walking.”

So what if some of what we call individual psychopathology is really a response to collective conditions that frustrate fundamental human needs?

Psychology should examine not only what patients are thinking and feeling but also take into account the influences that are causing people to think and feel the way they do. We should ask questions such as, “Do they have true agency? Are they physically engaged with the world? Do they experience meaningful relationships, belonging, creativity, and contribution? Do they have opportunities to experience spontaneity, wonder, and delight?”

Perhaps we need to reconsider the conditions under which we expect human beings to live, work, love, and flourish. That means examining not only individual choices but also workplaces, economic incentives, social institutions, and the technologies that increasingly mediate our experience of reality.

Helping people adapt to their circumstances is an important part of psychotherapy but our adaptation to COVID-lockdown reclusiveness may be more akin to zoochosis than we have hitherto believed.

Hari, J. (2022). "Stolen Focus: Why You Can't Pay Attention—and How to Think Deeply Again." Crown.
