#4632. Infant Bleeding Cases Surge as More Parents Refuse Vitamin K Shots for Newborns

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Two large studies published on November 5 link declining newborn vitamin K shot rates to a sharp increase in infant bleeding cases, including potentially fatal brain hemorrhages.

A research letter, published in JAMA Pediatrics, analyzed data on approximately 11 million infants from 2017 to 2025 and found that vitamin K administration declined from 97.7% to 95%, while cases of vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB) nearly quadrupled.

A second study published in JAMA, based on data from 5.2 million U.S. infants, found that refusal rates more than doubled, rising from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025. Infants who did not receive the shot had a 47% higher risk of bleeding and more than twice the risk of intracranial bleeding.

Additionally, new data from Truveta suggest the trend is continuing: refusals of vitamin K shots increased by 57% between January and June 2026, rising from 5.2% to 8.1% of newborns.

Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting, and newborns naturally have very low levels. Without the preventive injection, infants are at risk for VKDB, which can cause sudden bleeding in the brain, gastrointestinal tract, and other organs. Late-onset VKDB can occur up to six months after birth, often without warning signs, and may be fatal.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) continue to recommend an intramuscular vitamin K injection for all newborns, ideally within 6 hours of birth.

The shot is not a vaccine; it is a nutrient injection that helps prevent dangerous bleeding. A single dose reduces the risk of late-onset VKDB by approximately 98%.

Experts not involved in the studies attribute the rise in refusals partly to broader vaccine hesitancy and mixed public health messaging.

“The decision to vaccinate a newborn or allow a vitamin K injection at birth is complex, with multiple factors playing a role in the ultimate decision,” said Graham Tse, MD, a pediatrician and chief medical officer of MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, CA.

Some of these factors, Tse said, include conflicting messages from federal health agencies such as the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), both overseen by HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., an outspoken critic of the childhood immunization schedule.

The vitamin K shot is not a vaccine, yet RFK Jr. has declined to reassure parents about its safety, despite the CDC’s current recommendation to administer it at birth.

Additionally, growing medical distrust among parents has led to refusal of routine newborn care, such as the vitamin K shot, Reuters reports.

Healthline spoke with Tse to learn more about the risks of refusing the vitamin K shot and what new or expectant parents should know about this routine newborn treatment.

This interview has been lightly edited and condensed for clarity and length.

Tse: The decision to vaccinate a newborn or allow a vitamin K injection at birth is complex, with multiple factors playing a role in the ultimate decision.

A contributing factor to the decline in vitamin K injection at birth, as well as in newborn hepatitis B vaccination, is the conflicting messages from the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Recommendations from these entities and others are conflicting or do not align with established, research-based, and proven recommendations from organizations such as the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) and the Infectious Diseases Society of America.

When there are conflicting recommendations, it creates confusion and doubt among parents about what the best or right choice is for their child.

As well, there is so much misinformation on the internet, among influencers, and on social media that it is difficult to know what information is accurate, well-researched, and proven, versus what may be just someone’s opinion or belief.

Some are mistaking the vitamin K injection at birth for a vaccination, which it is not. Ultimately, all these factors are contributing to parents declining or delaying vitamin K injections at birth.

Tse: Declining the newborn vitamin K injection puts the newborn at significant risk of serious and life threatening complications from vitamin K-deficient bleeding (VKDB). This was previously referred to as hemorrhagic disease of the newborn.

VKDB can be as mild as bruising of the skin but can be as serious as bleeding into the brain, and newborns and infants can die from VKDB.

Declining vitamin K injection at birth is significant because of the serious and potentially life threatening consequences of deficiency of Vitamin K and not being able to clot the blood.

The vitamin K injection at birth is highly effective at preventing VKDB.

Tse: If a neonate or infant has vitamin K deficiency, the ability to clot their blood and stop bleeding is highly reduced.

All newborns are at risk of low vitamin K due to low body stores, low vitamin K content of breast milk, reduced ability of the gut to mobilize vitamin K, and poor transfer of vitamin K across the placenta.

When the blood cannot clot, bleeding from minor or minimal trauma can occur, and even bleeding without injury or trauma may occur. This can include bruises, bleeding from the mouth or gastrointestinal tract, bleeding from cuts or circumcision.

Bleeding can occur anywhere in the body, including in the brain, which can be catastrophic.

VKDB can occur from birth and through several months of life. Bleeding in the brain from VKDB, one of the most serious consequences, can occur at any time from birth to up to 6 months or so and can occur unexpectedly and suddenly. Vitamin K given at birth can prevent this risk of bleeding.

Tse: Vitamin K is a necessary vitamin that all humans need. Vitamin K is not a vaccination.

Newborns need vitamin K to prevent serious, significant, and often catastrophic bleeding during their first several months of life.

Vitamin K has been given to newborns in the United States for close to 70 years, is safe, is studied, and is proven to help prevent vitamin K-deficient bleeding.

I urge new parents to allow their newborns to receive the vitamin K injection at birth — it protects them, keeps them healthy, is proven safe, and is recommended.

#4629. Nuclear submarine returns from record-breaking 217 days underwater

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 16, 2026 1:05 PM EST

A nuclear submarine recently returned to Scotland after setting a Royal Navy record of 217 days underwater. The HMS Vengeance’s seven-month deployment overtook the 205-day milestone set by the HMS Vanguard in April. But with the Vengeance crew finally back home, critics now argue the two submarines’ lengthy back-to-back voyages are causes for concern, not celebration.

“The fleet was designed around three-month tours, and that was considered to be a long time to be stuck underwater in a metal box with no contact with the outside world,” nuclear submarine expert David Cullen told The Guardian on November 15.

The 17,526-ton, nearly 500-foot-long HMS Vengeance is one of Britain’s four Vanguard-class submarines constructed to carry monstrous Trident nuclear missiles. First launched in 1998, the vessel features 16 missile tubes, each loaded with one Trident containing up to a dozen, 100-kiloton multiple independently targetable reentry vehicles (MIRVs). The MIRV is specifically engineered to simultaneously deploy a payload of individual nuclear weapons aimed at a list of targets. The Royal Navy continuously keeps at least one Vanguard submarine at sea, which hypothetically allows the United Kingdom to still conduct nuclear strikes in the event its land-based systems are compromised during a nuclear war.

Vanguard submarines were originally built to host around 140 crewmembers during three-to-four month deployments. Although a 100-day excursion was once considered rare, underwater stints are now often double the length of time, forcing sailors to stack extra provisions along already cramped corridors and inside any additional nooks. The U.K. government attributes the extended missions to budgetary cuts that have dramatically slowed down the pace of multimillion-dollar vessel maintenance projects.

Deployment aboard a submarine like the Vengeance is considered one of the navy’s most psychologically difficult assignments. The nuclear sub remains underwater in total radio silence for the entire length of a patrol to keep its position secret. The vessel can travel to a depth of around 984 feet, but it may occasionally ascend to shallower waters to communicate via a transmission buoy or floating wire antenna. Crewmembers may receive a weekly, 120-word “Familygram” message, but each dispatch is previewed by naval officials. These readers retain the right to censor any bad news or information they feel may compromise sailors’ effectiveness. Regardless of what a sailor ultimately reads, they are strictly prohibited from responding.

The toll on crew is steep, but it’s particularly difficult for the women comprising roughly 10-percent of the navy. In 2022, whistleblower Sophie Brook generated international headlines after reporting a “constant campaign of sexual bullying” while serving as one of the Royal Navy’s first female submariners. In 2024, First Sea Lord Adm. Sir Ben Key called the crew misogyny “intolerable” and apologized to the growing number of women who subsequently came forward with their own stories. The Royal Navy’s investigations ultimately resulted in the firing, demotion, and disciplining of dozens of servicemen—including Key’s own termination.

Key’s successor, Gen. Sir Gwyn Jenkins, said he had “nothing but tremendous respect” for Trident crews earlier this month, while admitting the need to “improve our submarine maintenance.”

The Vanguard fleet was designed for about 25 years of service, but will likely accumulate roughly four decades of sailing by the time its first replacement is ready. That submarine, the HMS Dreadnought, isn’t expected to sail until around 2032.

#4628. Wild Conversations With Animals Foster Humility and Harmony

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 22, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

I'm always looking for books that foster a strong sense of community and connection with nonhuman animals. This is just what author Susan Beilby Magee does in her new book Wild Conversations: The Wisdom of African Animals, in which she shares wisdom and illuminates a path toward resilience, purpose, and harmony for all of Earth’s inhabitants. She also offers pertinent data from detailed research. Many of her positive messages reminded me of an interview I did with George Bumann about how eavesdropping on the wild conversations with different animals can offer lessons on the remarkable beings they are and what they need from us.

Marc Bekoff: Why did you write Wild Conversations?

Susan Beilby Magee: I wrote it because I made a promise to a lion. During a safari in northern Tanzania, I encountered a magnificent male lion walking through the bush. I greeted him silently and received a question in the intuitive way I have communicated with animals for decades: “Will you write a book about us? Will you share our messages with other humans?” I said: “Yes.”

That promise deepened over three African safaris. Their messages were wise, sometimes humorous, but grew urgent as wilderness habitats shrank. For example, lions have disappeared from more than 90 percent of their historic range, and research shows that only about 25 percent of Africa’s savannahs remain within the range of free-ranging lion populations. I wanted readers to encounter these animals not merely as tourist attractions on a safari, but as fellow beings with their own families, awareness, and place on Mother Earth. This book honors that promise.

SBM: I hope to reach animal lovers, conservationists, travelers, people curious about spirituality, and anyone who has felt renewed spending time in nature. I want to reach people overwhelmed by modern life. You need not believe in animal telepathy to recognize the intelligence and dignity of the animals. Although pollution, poaching, and human expansion threaten them, conservation can reverse some of the damage. For example, in Chad’s Zakouma National Park, where poaching had devastated the elephants, only one calf was counted in 2011. In 2018, due to intervention and protection by African Parks, 127 calves were counted. I want my granddaughter’s generation to see what is at stake. I hope readers finish with wonder, affection, and a desire to protect the wild.

MB: What are some of the topics you consider, and what are some of your major messages?

SBM: The book takes readers from the Serengeti and Tarangire to Ruaha and the Okavango Delta. I share personal encounters and photographs that explore animal wisdom, family life, interconnectedness, spiritual awareness, and conservation.

Our jeep once approached a herd of more than 200 elephants. The matriarch stopped, watched us, and directed the herd to surround the youngest calves. When I silently asked for her message, I heard: “Slow down. Don’t rush. Enjoy the moment. Love your family. Play together. Know that you, we, all life is eternal.” How many of us need a reminder to slow down? The message was not just a comfort, but also a warning: When we move as fast as so many of us do today, we often miss what really matters, whether it’s time with loved ones or confronting the harm we’re causing to the planet.

Other animals offered different lessons. A giraffe invited me to appreciate silence. A leopard encouraged spending time alone in nature and trusting our own inner resources. The hyenas urged purposeful work and devotion to one’s pack. And the lions reminded me to awaken my senses, appreciate beauty, and live with courage. Each message reflected its messenger.

There is also a harder truth: Life and death are interconnected. I watched wildebeest cross the Mara River as crocodiles waited, while predators, scavengers and insects each played a role. Death is natural. What we are doing to these animals is not.

In the book’s final section, Clarion Call, the messages become urgent. Habitat loss, pollution, and human expansion threaten these animals. I worry that lions, elephants, cheetahs and other magnificent creatures may disappear from the wild within my granddaughter’s lifetime. The population of Africa’s savanna elephants has fallen by at least 60 percent in 50 years, according to the IUCN. My central appeal is both spiritual and practical: Reconnect with Mother Earth, recognize that we belong to the same living community, and act to protect the places these animals call home

MB: How does your book differ from others concerned with similar topics?

SBM: Wild Conversations is neither a scientific field guide nor a conventional safari memoir. I write as a modern mystic, sharing the messages I personally experienced through silent, intuitive communication with animals. Readers may interpret these encounters differently; I welcome that. I simply invite them to pay attention.

The foreword is by Michael Lorentz, a wildlife photographer who has guided African safaris for 40 years. He writes that the animals are “far more present, far more aware, and far more communicative than most of us are conditioned to believe.” Frank Pope, CEO of Save the Elephants, has endorsed the book, calling it “A passionate love-letter to the wild.” You don’t have to be a mystic to appreciate the book’s photographs and messages.

MB: Are you hopeful that learning more about these animals will inspire greater action to save them and the African wilderness?

SBM: Yes. I hope people will protect wild animals and wilderness worldwide. When we watch an elephant protect her calf or lion cubs tumble together in play, the distance between “us” and “them” begins to disappear. We see families, relationships, and individual lives. That recognition can lead to respect, and respect can lead to stewardship. I want my granddaughter and all future generations to inherit a world where wild lions still roar, elephants still roam, and the Serengeti remains alive with migrating herds.

In conversation with Susan Beilby Magee, an author, activist and modern mystic whose career spans politics, business, government and spirituality. A leader in Seattle’s women’s movement in the 1970s, she served as a White House Fellow under President Gerald Ford and later became an international business consultant. She holds an MBA from the Wharton School and a BA from Pomona College.

#4626. FDA Initiates Labeling Changes for GLP-1s Due to Rare But Serious Eye Disease Risk

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

GLP-1 users have a new symptom to watch for: Sudden vision loss in one eye.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) announced on November 9 that it will require drugmakers to add information to the warning labels of Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, Zepbound and other GLP-1 medications about “a potential increased risk” of a rare eye condition called nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION).GLP-1 medications are approved to treat type 2 diabetes and to help people lose weight and keep it off.NAION joins a growing list of side effects linked to GLP-1s, adding a second eye warning to several labels.The U.S. labels for Ozempic, Rybelsus, Trulicity, Mounjaro, and Zepbound already warn about diabetic retinopathy, a diabetes-related eye disease, according to each drug’s prescribing information.The two conditions affect different parts of the eye. Diabetic retinopathy damages tiny blood vessels in the retina, the layer at the back of the eye that senses light, according to the National Eye Institute. NAION damages the optic nerve when it doesn’t get enough blood, according to the FDA’s announcement.Mihail Zilbermint, MD, director of endocrine hospitalists at Johns Hopkins, told Healthline he hasn’t seen NAION in his patients. He has seen vision worsen in some people after they start a GLP-1.“But we believe that’s probably related to rapid improvement in their sugar control, which can also be seen in someone who is starting insulin,” Zilbermint said.

A 2024 study published in JAMA Ophthalmology “initially triggered” the FDA’s review, the agency told Healthline.

The study found a higher risk of NAION in people prescribed semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, than in people prescribed other diabetes or weight-loss drugs.The authors wrote that more research is needed to determine whether semaglutide causes NAION.Joseph F. Rizzo III, MD, director of the Neuro-Ophthalmology Service at Mass Eye and Ear in Boston, served as the study’s corresponding author.

In a 2024 podcast, Rizzo said he and a resident saw three patients with NAION who were taking semaglutide for about a week.“And because NAION is a fairly uncommon disorder in the general population, the fact that we had three within a relatively short period of time led me to suspect that there was a higher risk of developing NAION in patients on semaglutide,” Rizzo said. The FDA analyzed clinical trials for multiple GLP-1 drugs and noted that NAION cases were reported with every GLP-1 on the market, according to its announcement. Those findings led the FDA to require the warning for the entire drug class, the agency told Healthline.

About 70% to 80% of people with NAION first notice vision loss when they wake up, according to StatPearls. The FDA listed these symptoms:

No treatment has been proven to reverse vision loss from NAION, according to StatPearls.

“Patients experiencing sudden, painless vision loss in one eye should contact their healthcare professional immediately and should not stop their medication without consulting their provider first,” the FDA told Healthline.

In the announcement, the agency told doctors to promptly refer patients with suspected NAION to an ophthalmologist.

The FDA listed these possible risk factors for NAION:

The FDA told Healthline that many people who take GLP-1s also have these conditions, which made reports of NAION in GLP-1 users “challenging” to interpret.

Across 126 clinical trials, the FDA found about 6 NAION cases per 100,000 people taking a GLP-1 for a year, and about 4 per 100,000 people taking a placebo or another diabetes drug for a year.In real-world data, NAION was more common with GLP-1s than with one type of diabetes pill, but the FDA found no significant increase compared with another type, the agency told Healthline.Zilbermint said patients who saw the news have worried about losing their vision. He tells them that “many of the serious harms, including the potential harm of NAION, are rare.”“The overall risk is still very small,” he said.

Regulators in other countries have added NAION warnings, mostly for semaglutide:

The FDA told Healthline the benefits of GLP-1s “continue to outweigh their risks when used as directed.”The FDA has also approved some GLP-1s to lower the risk of heart attack and stroke, reduce the risk of worsening kidney disease, and treat sleep apnea and a type of liver disease.Zilbermint said that “for most of my patients with obesity, diabetes and heart disease, the benefits clearly outweigh the risks.”“But we definitely have to decide patient by patient,” he added.

The labeling change applies to these medications, according to the FDA’s announcement:

As of publication, the FDA’s online label database did not yet show the new warning on the drugs’ labels.

#4624. Tesla on Autopilot/FSD hit an overturned truck at 71 mph, killing 3

A Tesla Model 3 drove into an overturned box truck on I-75 near Naples, Florida, killing two of its passengers and a man who had stopped to help. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators says Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, at 71 mph.

Police and local media covered the May 31 crash as a truck wreck in the dark, and none of it mentioned a driver-assist system. It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data, and it lands as Tesla’s monthly crash count hits another record.

Just before 4 a.m. on Sunday, May 31, 2026, the 31-year-old driver of a 2014 Freightliner lost the road near the Pine Ridge Road exit in Collier County, steered back onto southbound I-75, and flipped it, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The overturned truck ended up blocking the center and outside lanes.

Jonathan Garcia Arias, a 25-year-old Naples man and former Marine, was driving by in a BMW. He pulled over and got out to help the truck driver.

Then a southbound 2023 Tesla with five young men from Naples inside came up on the scene. FHP’s report says the front of the Tesla hit the underside of the overturned truck and Garcia Arias. Two of the Tesla’s passengers, aged 18 and 19, died at the scene, and Garcia Arias died later in the hospital. The 20-year-old driver and two more passengers were seriously hurt.

A few days later, FHP used the crash as a warning about stopping near wrecks on the interstate. Senior Trooper Kenn Watson said the Tesla driver would have seen only the truck’s underside, with “no lights, no reflectors, nothing warning them.”

So that’s the official story. A dark obstacle, a driver who couldn’t see it in time. Nobody said a word about Autopilot.

Under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone was killed or hurt. Tesla filed one for this crash.

It identifies the car as a 2023 Model 3 on a highway, flags a traffic incident on the roadway, and marks the automation “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That means Tesla confirmed through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 71 mph and a fatality, lists the Florida Highway Patrol as the investigating agency, and says it learned of the crash from police and the media.

Then it blacks out the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was within the system’s approved operating domain, all as “confidential business information.” That’s the same redaction Tesla applies to 99.9% of its reports.

The report also surfaced late. Tesla filed it as a 5-Day report, the urgent category for fatal crashes, but it didn’t land until Tesla’s September filings, more than three months after the crash. And Tesla lists law enforcement as one of the ways it found out about it.

How we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 07:56 UTC, which converts to 3:56 a.m. in Florida, two minutes off the 3:54 a.m. in FHP’s report. The city, the highway, the 2023 model year, the month and the fatal outcome all line up, and it’s the only fatal Tesla driver-assist report in Naples that month. It’s the same crash.

A Tesla on driver-assist going highway speed into the underside of a big truck, in the dark, in Florida. If that sounds familiar, it should.

In 2016, Joshua Brown was killed near Williston when his Model S on Autopilot drove under a tractor-trailer crossing the highway. In 2019, Jeremy Banner died in Delray Beach when his Model 3 on Autopilot went under a trailer at 68 mph and had its roof sheared off. In both crashes, neither the driver nor the system braked.

Trooper Watson’s point was that a human couldn’t see the truck. But a big, unlit obstacle sitting across two lanes at night is exactly the kind of thing a driver-assist system is supposed to catch, and Tesla now sells FSD as nearly ready to drive with nobody watching. And an attentive driver could clearly see it, as the BMW driver did, and stop before the Tesla arrived.

We want to be fair about what the data doesn’t prove. “Engaged within 30 seconds” is the reporting trigger. Tesla’s 71 mph may be a telematics snapshot rather than the impact speed. And with the software version redacted, we can’t say whether this was Autopilot or FSD.

The NHTSA release that surfaced this crash, covering filings through October 15, also set a new monthly high. Tesla reported 264 driver-assist crashes in September 2026, beating July’s 236, which was itself a record. That’s up from 135 in March.

September may still grow as late reports come in. This Naples crash shows how late they can be.

Our merged dataset now holds 4,669 Tesla driver-assist crash reports since 2019, 69 of them flagged fatal. The same release added two other fatal reports, both “Verified Engaged” and both covered locally with no mention of driver-assist: a Model Y that hit a tree and burned in El Dorado Hills, California, killing three, and a Model X that hit a signal pole in Naples on September 30, killing a passenger. We’ll lay those out separately.

Three people died on I-75, including a man who got out of his car to help a stranger. Tesla knows its driver-assist was on, knows the speed, holds the telematics, and filed a federal report saying so. Then it sealed everything that would explain what the car did, and the public got a story about a dark truck.

That's what happens when the system has to identify all objects in the camera frame before it can start to estimate the objects position and then relative distance and then relative velocity. Unrecognizable objects will destroy all your logic. This is a design failure and not something Tesla can actually fix.

Compare that to radars and lidars that directly measure distances and relative velocities of everything in front of the car, regardless of what it is. That is a far better approach because you do not want the car the impact objects on its trajectory regardless of what those objects turn out to be.

Tesla’s whole pitch for FSD is that the car sees better than you do, and yet, Tesla vehicles on Autopilot and FSD keep crashing on stationary objects on the highway. It’s the same failure that killed Joshua Brown and Jeremy Banner years ago. If the system saw the truck and the driver overrode it, Tesla should say so. It was quick to do that in the Katy crash when the data helped it. If the system didn’t see it, that’s a safety defect regulators and owners need to know about.

Either way, the redaction protects Tesla, not the people on the road. It’s the same pattern we found in Vineland and in July’s four fatal crashes, and the crash count keeps setting records.

We’re asking the Florida Highway Patrol for the full crash report, whether its investigators got Tesla’s raw vehicle data, and whether they even knew the system was engaged. If they didn’t, the only party that knows what this car did is the one that sealed the file.

#4623. Why Does Life Feel Absurd?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 22, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader

“MOST people feel on occasion that life is absurd, and some feel it vividly and continually” is how Thomas Nagel opens his paper "The Absurd," yet "they could not really explain why life is absurd. Why then do they provide a natural expression for the sense that it is?” This is why I've recently published an academic article on the topic.

What then is the absurd? As Albert Camus is most often associated with the term the absurd, I will begin with his account. He begins by illustrating the common uses of the word absurd and gives the example of a virtuous man, who we accuse of desiring his sister. Naturally, he would respond in shock: “That is absurd!” Thereby appealing to the “contradictory” and “impossible” notion of the accusation, like a man attacking a group of gunmen with a sword. The intention of the action clashes with the harsh reality, thereby rendering the whole endeavor absurd. For Camus, the “absurd is born of this confrontation between the human need [for meaning and reason] and the unreasonable silence of the world.”

The feeling of the absurd therefore stems from two realizations taken together. First, man’s realization that life is meaningless and the universe purposeless; and secondly, man’s desire for meaning and purpose. The absurd is the futile search for meaning. It is neither existential nihilism that is absurd, nor the human search for meaning, but the comparison, the conflict, that arises between them.

Let us now take a look at an analytical philosopher, i.e., Thomas Nagel and his paper “The Absurd." Nagel, too, starts from the notion of the absurd in ordinary life, giving a similar analysis to Camus’, stating that it “includes a conspicuous discrepancy between pretension or aspiration and reality," like someone giving a complex speech on a vote that has already been cast. A philosophical notion of absurdity, in contrast to the feeling of absurdity, however, must according to Nagel lie in “something universal-some respect in which pretension and reality inevitably clash for us all” and that is a “collision between the seriousness with which we take our lives and the perpetual possibility of regarding everything about which we are serious as arbitrary, or open to doubt.”

As one might argue goes, “why struggle, if the struggle doesn’t amount to anything?” This question is unique for humans, in that only they have the ability to take a step back and look at themselves from a grander point of view, which is seemingly impossible for animals. From this perspective, our lives must appear “sobering and comical.” As Nagel says:

We step back to find that the whole system of justification and criticism, which controls our choices and supports our claims to rationality, rests on responses and habits that we never question, that we should not know how to defend without circularity, and to which we shall continue to adhere even after they are called into question.

Our aims and goals must from this perspective appear arbitrary. They are, in the end, so small and insignificant that one can only wonder why we put so much energy into achieving our life goals. This is the absurd condition we cannot escape.

We must, therefore, acknowledge that the “absurdity of our situation derives not from a collision between our expectations and the world, but from a collision within ourselves.” I don’t agree with Nagel, in his claim to provide a superior account to that of Camus. If anything, Nagel reinforces Camus’ argument. For Camus as for Nagel, the search for final justifications in God, religion, power, family or the state is just as futile, for their purposes must appear just as absurd if we take a step back. They are no more than an escape from the absurd, not a solution. For now, it seems as if Camus’ notion of the absurd is compatible with contemporary analytical philosophy after all.

If you enjoyed this short essay, you might enjoy the much longer version, on which it is based, where I go into much more detail: click here.

Veit, W. (2018). Existential Nihilism: The Only Really Serious Philosophical Problem. Journal of Camus Studies 2018, 211–236. https://doi.org/10.13140/RG.2.2.26965.24804 [Download]

Browning, H., & Veit, W. (2022). The Desperate Search for Meaning in Life. In C. Cotton & A. M. Winters (Eds.), Neon Genesis Evangelion and Philosophy (pp. 3–12). Chicago: Carus Books. [Download]

Camus, A. (1955). The Myth of Sisyphus (J. O’Brien, Trans.). London: Hamish Hamilton. (Original work published 1942)

Nagel, T. (1971). The absurd. The Journal of Philosophy, 68(20), 716–727.

#4622. Tesla on Autopilot/FSD was going 74 mph before fiery crash that killed 3

A Tesla Model Y left a parkway in El Dorado Hills, California, hit a tree and burst into flames in September, killing three of the four people inside. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators says Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, with the car doing 74 mph.

The crash was widely covered in the Sacramento area as a fiery single-car wreck. None of that coverage mentioned a driver-assist system. It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data.

Late on Saturday, September 12, 2026, a 2024 Tesla Model Y with four people inside was heading west on Serrano Parkway, between Terracina Drive and Silva Valley Parkway. That’s a residential part of the Serrano community in El Dorado Hills, east of Sacramento.

According to the CHP’s Placerville office, the Model Y left the road “for unknown reasons,” hit a tree on the north side of the parkway, and caught fire. Officers got the call around 10:38 p.m. By the time they arrived, the car was fully engulfed in flames.

Charles Anthony Cameron, 30, of Sacramento, was thrown from the car and died at the scene. Alejandra Mendoza, 28, of Sacramento, and Kailauna Viola Mills, 28, of Roseville, were found dead inside once firefighters put out the fire. One of the two women was driving; CHP hasn’t publicly said which.

Mills lived in Arizona and was visiting family. Her uncle told CBS Sacramento she worked in the medical field and was supposed to get married next April.

A fourth person, a 28-year-old Sacramento woman, survived with major injuries.

CHP says the cause is still under investigation. Speed, impairment, and how the car left the road haven’t been released. And nobody has said a word about Autopilot.

Under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone is killed or hurt. Tesla filed a report on this one.

It lists a 2024 Model Y, a consumer vehicle, and marks the “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That’s Tesla confirming through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 74 mph, a fatality, and the California Highway Patrol as the investigating agency.

Then it redacts the narrative, the software version, and whether the road was inside the system’s operating domain, all as “confidential business information,” the same treatment Tesla gives 99.9% of its reports.

The rest of the report is strangely thin. Tesla lists the roadway type as “Unknown” and what the car hit as “Unknown,” even though police said it was a tree. It checks only one source for how it learned of the crash: the media. So Tesla found out about a triple-fatal crash in one of its cars from the news, then went into its own data and confirmed its driver-assist was on.

How we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 05:36 UTC, which is 10:36 p.m. Pacific on September 12, within two minutes of the 10:38 p.m. call CHP responded to. The city, the 2024 Model Y, the month, and the fatal outcome all line up. It’s the only fatal Tesla driver-assist report from El Dorado Hills in the data. It’s the same crash.

Two of the three victims were found inside the car after the fire was out. The survivor got out of, or was pulled from, the wreckage, depending on the report.

CHP hasn’t said whether the doors played any role, and we’re not suggesting they did. But it’s a fair question to ask about any Tesla crash with a fire, now that NHTSA is writing new rules for emergency door releases after years of complaints about people getting trapped. We’ve asked.

This is the second triple-fatal crash in Tesla’s latest NHTSA filings where its driver-assist was verified engaged and the public never heard about it. The other one was on I-75 in Naples. Add Vineland and July’s four fatal crashes, and the pattern is hard to miss.

"what little effort went into the report"?

I disagree, a lot of effort went in to minimize the report, to portray it as an unremarkable accident.

That is the effort I find Tesla criminally responsible for.

The CHP need the full report, no redactions. If they chose to censor it that is their task, not Tesla's.

What stands out in this one is how little effort went into the report. Tesla knows the speed, knows the system was on, and has telematics. But it couldn’t fill in what the car hit, and it learned about three deaths in one of its cars from the news. Then it redacted the one field, the narrative, that would tell us what the car did.

Tesla wants regulators and customers to trust FSD with no one watching. That trust has to be earned with data. A company that seals the account of what its car did at 74 mph in a neighborhood, in a crash that killed three people, isn’t earning it.

We’re asking CHP Placerville whether its investigators knew the system was engaged, whether they got Tesla’s raw data or Tesla’s summary of it, and what they found about the fire and the doors. If CHP never got the full data, how will it ever determine the cause?

#4621. Peeping woodcocks are evolutionary oddballs

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 16, 2026 3:00 PM EST

As far as birds go, the eight known species of woodcock (genus Scolopax) look like they specifically evolved to go viral on the internet. You’ve probably seen at least a few videos of the birds on social media darting across beaches and being incredibly vocal. As if their small, squat bodies and comically long beaks weren’t enough, they also vocalize with distinctively cartoonish peeping tweets during their mating displays.

Woodcocks are part of the larger sandpiper family, but unlike their migratory relatives, most only travel extremely short seasonal distances. Six of the eight species are only found on specific islands, and some of them don’t even migrate at all. So how did these evolutionary oddballs even get their start—and stop migrating? To piece together their unique avian story, biologists analyzed the DNA of all eight woodcock species and 22 species of snipe.

“The distribution of woodcocks and snipes around the world is really unusual,” John Bates, the curator of birds at the Field Museum’s Negaunee Integrative Research Center in Chicago, said in a statement. “They’re not terribly aerodynamic, and yet they’ve clearly gotten around.”

Bates and his colleagues published the results of their work today in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS). The years-long endeavor involved not only examining preserved woodcock specimens housed in the Field Museum, but a fossilized sandpiper previously excavated from a cave site in Haiti. The remains found on the island of Hispaniola are around 1,000 years old, but that is still extremely young in the grand history of shorebirds.

The earliest members of the sandpiper family began in the northern hemisphere before slowly migrating to islands along lower latitudes. Those birds subsequently migrated much shorter distances after settling in the warmer climates. However, they didn’t remain sedentary. Based on the DNA analysis detailed in their study, Bates and his team theorize that snipes from Africa eventually traveled across the Atlantic Ocean, then evolved into new species in South America. From there, more of the birds made their way over the Pacific Ocean to New Zealand.

Their examinations also cleared up a bit of confusion. Biologists initially believed the fossilized sandpiper from Haiti was a woodcock, but the most recent data now shows that it’s a snipe.

“Snipes and woodcocks have been around for 20 to 25 million years,” Bates explained. “Over that time, as new species have evolved and moved around the world, their migratory patterns have changed, too.”

These changes are likely to continue amid today’s dramatic climate shifts, but that may pose a problem for the beloved woodcocks.

“These are definitely birds that would be affected by changing habitats and changing climates,” said Bates. “Some of these woodcocks are found only in the mountain forests on islands between Asia and Australia, and if those forests get cut down, the birds are going to be gone too.”

#4620. 1 in 3 Infants Diagnosed With Peanut Allergy May Not Have the Condition

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Peanut allergies have been on the rise in recent decades.

According to statistics provided by Food Allergy Research & Education (FARE), an estimated 6.2 million children and adults in the United States are allergic to peanuts.

However, new research published in the November 2026 issue of The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology suggests that over a third of infants thought to have this diagnosis might not actually have a peanut allergy.

In fact, having a history of reacting to peanuts and positive allergy testing on their own may not be sufficient to diagnose a peanut allergy for many infants.

The study’s authors suggest that a threshold oral food challenge — in which the child is given increasing amounts of the suspected food allergen under medical supervision to look for an allergic reaction — should be routinely considered to help confirm peanut allergy.

This additional testing could safely prevent children who are not allergic to peanuts from undergoing unnecessary treatment with oral immunotherapy.

It could also spare families from burdensome food restrictions and allergy precautions.

The researchers’ goal was to evaluate the accuracy and safety of the Allergy Development to an Accelerated Path to Tolerance (ADAPT) peanut oral immunotherapy program, which was established in 2024 at 10 public children’s hospitals across Australia.

This program provides a standardized approach to evaluating and treating infants with suspected peanut allergies.

The study included infants who had experienced a mild to moderate reaction to peanut before 12 months of age and had evidence of peanut sensitization through allergy testing.

Researchers reviewed medical records to examine how accurately the program’s approach identified peanut allergies and whether it could safely guide treatment.

A key part of the evaluation was a threshold oral food challenge. The challenge involved up to seven doses, ranging from 15 to 1,300 milligrams of peanut protein.

Medical teams monitored the infants for reactions and provided treatment when necessary.

Researchers reviewed records from April 2024 through October 2025. During that period, 1,275 infants were assessed through the program, and 778 underwent an oral food challenge.

The researchers also examined allergy test results and whether infants who reacted during the challenges could begin oral immunotherapy at an appropriate starting dose.

At the time of the oral food challenge, the infants had a median age of 13 months.

Of the 778 infants who underwent an oral food challenge, 507 (65.2%) had an allergic reaction.

However, 271 (34.8%) did not react to peanut during the supervised test, despite having a history of a previous reaction and positive allergy test results.

These findings suggest that relying on medical history and allergy tests alone may lead some infants to be labeled with a peanut allergy when they can actually tolerate the food.

Among the infants who reacted during the challenges, 61 experienced anaphylaxis, a severe allergic reaction that can affect breathing and blood pressure. This represented 12% of infants with a positive challenge and 7.8% of all infants who underwent testing. Medical teams safely managed these severe allergic reactions.

Researchers also found that infants who reacted to peanut generally had higher skin prick test results and Ara h 2-specific IgE levels than those who did not react.

However, these test results did not reliably indicate how much peanut would trigger a reaction or how severe that reaction would be.

Of the 394 infants who began peanut oral immunotherapy, 384 (97.5%) successfully started treatment at a dose below the amount that had triggered a reaction during their food challenge.

The researchers say these findings support considering supervised oral food challenges to confirm suspected peanut allergies before starting treatment or recommending long-term avoidance.

Erin Banta, MD, a board certified allergist and immunologist who treats both children and adults at Latitude Food Allergy Care in Great Neck, New York, said these findings are significant because they provide evidence for early use of oral food challenges in infants with peanut reactions.

“In those with mild-moderate prior reactions to peanut, early oral food challenge may allow for either delabeling of food allergy (in 1/3 of the patients in this study) or diagnosis of food allergy,” she told Healthline.

Banta, who wasn’t involved in the study, added that early delabeling takes a significant burden off the patient and their family.

“On the other hand,” she explained, “early diagnosis allows for early initiation of treatment with oral immunotherapy at a time in the patient’s life associated with the greatest success rates.”

Banta further noted that the study offers different pathways for oral immunotherapy based on the patient’s reaction threshold. This means that some patients may be able to complete treatment more quickly due to their individual threshold dose.

Lindsey Forstie, FNP, a family nurse practitioner with clinical training and experience in allergy and asthma care at Carefree Allergy in Phoenix, AZ, added that while further evaluation may be needed to confirm a peanut allergy diagnosis, it’s important for parents not to try introducing peanuts at home.

“Instead, they should speak with their pediatrician or allergist about appropriate testing and whether a supervised food challenge is safe and necessary,” she said.

According to Forstie, who was also not part of the study, the goal is to avoid unnecessary food restrictions while also keeping children safe.

“The key message is that not every positive allergy test means a child has a food allergy,” she told Healthline. “Accurate diagnosis helps protect children while allowing those who are not allergic to enjoy a more normal, less restrictive diet.”

#4619. The Ache of Feeling Overlooked

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 22, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader

We never really know what someone else is carrying in their backpack of rocks. One of my former colleagues, a brilliant consultant, springs to mind. She was highly experienced, calmly present under pressure, and one of those people a hospital comes to depend upon without anyone saying as much.

Younger doctors would seek her out after shifts and, though she never gave much overt advice, when she spoke they paid attention. Usually she listened carefully, asked a question, or helped them see what had just happened from a new perspective. She was also the last person who would have wanted a fuss made of her.

At some point, she started to change. Nothing dramatic, and she still came to work and took care of her patients as diligently and professionally as ever. If you'd asked me then whether anything was noticeably wrong, I am embarrassed to admit that I would probably have dismissed it. On reflection, I can see that she'd stopped staying behind after teaching sessions to chat with students. She also spoke less in meetings and our general conversations became shorter. She was responding to other colleagues differently too, but we were all over-extended and too preoccupied to rally round.

I assumed she was tired. Nothing unusual about that in a hospital, after all. I never asked her directly what was going on, so I don't know. Maybe she had problems at home, or just decided to work less, and I would be doing her a disservice if I invented a reason for her withdrawal all these years later. What haunts me is that I noticed the change and didn't stop to ask why. She left the hospital soon after.

Doctors spend years learning to observe people. We study skin color, breathing, posture and movement. We become experts at listening to how people speak and notice when their account doesn't quite fit what we are seeing in front of us. Sometimes a tiny detail changes the direction of an examination.

I'm less certain that we are equally observant of the people working alongside us. Hospitals are notoriously busy places, and when someone continues to show up, doing good work and causing us no interruptions, our attention naturally goes elsewhere. This is particularly the case with competent people, and when we are so cocooned in our own work with all its decisions and distractions, it's not so easy to notice when a colleague interacts less or keeps their door closed. Any one of these signals could mean absolutely nothing, but if you know someone well enough to spot their behavior has changed, why not ask? I wish I had.

Years later, I came across a study by Naomi Eisenberger, Matthew Lieberman, and Kipling Williams that made me reconsider that colleague. The researchers used brain imaging to study what happened when people experienced social exclusion during a virtual ball-tossing game. They found activity in some of the brain regions also involved in the distress of physical pain.

The study was published in Science in 2003 and has since generated a good deal of research and discussion. A brain scan can't tell us what my colleague was experiencing, of course. I cannot say whether she felt personally excluded, though the study piqued my interest in something I had previously underestimated: how much being included matters to us.

You don't have to be physically alone to be lonely. I've known several people who have spent their lives elbow-deep in friends, family and colleagues, but who still feel disconnected from others. In a large hospital, and I'm sure in other workplaces, it's perfectly possible to speak to dozens of people every day, without enjoying a conversation where someone asks how you are and genuinely wants to hear the answer.

I used to believe that recognition was mainly about acknowledging exemplary work, but I'm no longer sure that's accurate. Praise has its place, and most of us like to hear what we did well, but in the difficult phases of my own life, the times I've felt truly noticed have been thanks to interactions that are much more subtle. Somebody maybe remembers a joke or a fact I told them weeks ago, or a colleague checks in when I'm unusually quiet. Occasionally a friend will hesitate and ask again after enquiring how I am and receiving the classic response 'Fine.'

None of these moments of recognition would appear in an organizational strategy. They cost nothing and can take less than a minute, but they tell us something valuable: someone has put their own busyness aside long enough to truly care.

Healthcare organizations spend time and money figuring out how to best care for patients, as they should. I wonder if we forget to look sideways at the people providing that care. Who pays attention to them? The people I worry about most aren't necessarily those who announce they're struggling. Often it's the person who just gets on with the job without complaining, who continues to do an excellent job while gradually becoming harder to reach.

I still have no idea what happened to the consultant I worked alongside all those years ago. I only know that I noticed her withdrawal and attributed it to tiredness. If I found myself in the same situation today, I hope I would be attentive enough to knock on the door of her office, sit down and ask how she was, and actually wait long enough for the answer.

Eisenberger, N. I., Lieberman, M. D., & Williams, K. D. (2003). Does rejection hurt? An fMRI study of social exclusion. Science, 302(5643), 290–292.

Published Nov 16, 2026 4:07 PM EST

Over the past 17 months, the Wildlife Conservation Society’s Bronx Zoo in New York City has rescued dozens of parrots from the illegal pet trade. They include white-fronted Amazons (Amazona albifrons) and orange-fronted conures (Eupsittula canicularis).

The United States Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) confiscated the orange-fronted conures during three separate operations over the last 17 months, and the white-fronted Amazons in the last several months. All of the birds were discovered at the U.S.–Mexico border.

“These animals were stolen from the wild and are victims of the illegal wildlife pet trade, and our responsibility is to give them the best possible chance for a healthy future,” Chuck Cerbini, WCS Bronx Zoo Curator of Ornithology, said in a statement. “Working with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, our veterinary and animal care teams provide specialized expertise to assess, treat, and care for confiscated wildlife.”

When confiscated wildlife arrives at the Bronx Zoo, the veterinary and animal care teams first conduct a health check, provide any necessary medical treatment, and then help find long-term placements for those that can’t be released into the wild.

White-fronted Amazons are native to parts of Mexico and Central America and represent the smallest Amazon parrot. They are also one of the few parrot species in which males and females feature visibly different plumage. Both sexes have a white foreheads, red faces, and yellowish bills, but males have red shoulders and females have green shoulders.

Orange-fronted conures, also known as half-moon conure or Petz’s conure, are also native to parts of Mexico and Central America, where they live in open woodlands, forest edges, and savannas. They have an orange forehead and green and blue feathers.

The IUCN Red List categorizes both birds as a species of Least Concern, but that still  doesn’t justify trafficking them in the illegal pet trade. Parrots throughout Latin America are subject to both the loss of forest habitat and poaching.

Birds in particular l are especially threatened by trafficking because they are valued in the pet trade and the collector trade.

#4616. High Fat Diet Linked to Higher Colon Cancer Risk, Early Research Shows

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

In a new study, researchers report that a high fat diet may potentially increase the risk of colon cancer.

The researchers from Arizona State University said a diet high in certain fats can cause lasting changes in intestinal stem cells that lead to the development of tumors and the possibility of colon cancer.

The study was conducted in mice, but the researchers noted changes in the DNA of intestinal stem cells that may explain their growth and survival.

The researchers published their findings on November 12 in the journal Stem Cell Reports.

The researchers said the study is important because 1 in 25 people develop colon cancer in their lifetime. In the United States, that translates into about 108,000 new cases of colon cancer every year. About 55,000 males and 55,000 females are expected to die from the disease in 2026.

Experts not involved in the study say the research provides valuable information, but they have reservations about the results, as the findings do not yet apply to humans.

“The findings provide a potential mechanism linking diet to intestinal cancer development, but we need to be cautious about translating these results to humans,” said Dalia Perelman, MS, CDE, a research dietitian at Stanford University in California.

“We already have evidence from human studies that obesity and certain dietary patterns, particularly those high in processed meats and low in fiber-rich foods, are associated with increased colorectal cancer risk,” Perelman told Healthline. “This study adds a potentially important mechanism to investigate, but it does not establish that dietary fat itself increases colorectal cancer risk in humans.”

Ketan Thanki, MD, a colorectal surgeon specializing in benign and malignant diseases of the colon, rectum, and anus at the MemorialCare Todd Cancer Institute at Long Beach Medical Center in California, shared similar views.

“This study provides a better understanding at the cellular level of how a high fat diet may contribute to colorectal cancer development,” Thanki told Healthline.

“Animal studies are an important starting point for understanding biological processes, but we must be cautious about directly applying their findings to humans,” he added. “Mice and humans share many cellular and biological mechanisms, which makes these studies valuable in identifying potential pathways involved in disease development. However, human diets, genetics, metabolism, and environmental exposures are more complex.”

To reach their findings, the Arizona State researchers fed mice what the scientists described as a Western-style high fat diet for 6 months.

They then compared those results with those from mice given a low fat diet.

The researchers said the mice on the high fat diet gained more weight than the mice on the low-fat diet. They also developed more intestinal stem cells, and those cells grew at a more rapid rate.

They added that mice genetically predisposed to intestinal cancer who were fed a high-fat diet developed more and larger tumors.

The researchers noted changes in the DNA of intestinal stem cells that may help explain their increased growth and survival.

They also pointed out that stem cell behavior returned to normal after high fat diet mice were switched to a low fat diet, although some DNA changes persisted. After four weeks, approximately 18% of these changes remained.

When mice were returned to a high fat diet, the researchers said their intestinal stem cells responded more quickly and strongly than those of mice exposed to the diet for the first time.

They concluded that the study suggests that maintaining a healthy, low fat diet may help regulate intestinal stem cell growth and reduce colon cancer risk.

Kristin Kirkpatrick, RD, president of KAK Consulting and a dietitian at the Cleveland Clinic Department of Wellness & Preventive Medicine in Ohio, wasn’t involved in the study but highlighted a particular aspect of the findings.

“What I found particularly interesting was that even after the mice returned to a low fat diet, some of the molecular changes persisted,” she told Healthline. “This raises questions about how our dietary patterns over time may influence long-term health.”

Experts said these new findings are interesting but noted numerous caveats.

“One important takeaway is that dietary habits over time matter,” said Thanki. “Even if someone has consumed a high fat diet for years, making changes now may still provide meaningful health benefits.”

“I also think these findings are particularly important for children and adolescents, as establishing healthier dietary habits early in life may provide long-term benefits,” he added.

However, Thanki noted that not all fats are the same. “The health risks depend partly on the type of fat consumed, how much is consumed, and what foods make up the overall diet,” he said.

“Diets consistently high in saturated fats, particularly those containing large amounts of processed meats, fried foods, and highly processed products, can contribute to obesity, elevated cholesterol, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic dysfunction. These factors can also contribute to chronic inflammation and may increase the risk of certain cancers, including colorectal cancer,” Thanki continued.

Perelman said the diet used in the study was extremely high in fat, providing 60% of calories from fat, primarily from lard.

“We know that the health effects of dietary fats differ depending on their sources and fatty acid composition, and we cannot assume that a diet rich in unsaturated fats from foods such as olive oil, nuts, and seeds would produce the same effects,” she noted.

Perelman added that the researchers primarily studied stem cells from the small intestine rather than the colon.

“Although these tissues share some biological characteristics, they have important differences, and we cannot assume that the same changes would occur in the colon,” she explained.

Finally, Perelman noted that “the mice consuming the high fat diet also gained weight, making it difficult to separate the effects of dietary fat itself from those associated with increased body fat and other metabolic changes.”

Not all high fat foods are unhealthy. Some high fat foods that offer healthy benefits include:

“The goal shouldn’t necessarily be to eliminate fat because our bodies need healthy fats for normal functioning,” said Thanki. “Instead, people should focus on reducing saturated and trans fats while incorporating healthier unsaturated fats in appropriate amounts.”

Thanki had several dietary suggestions. Among them:

“Consistency matters more than perfection. Even modest dietary changes, maintained over time, can have meaningful health benefits,” Thanki said.

Perelman agreed. “The overall quality of the diet matters. Diets that are very high in fat may displace other foods and nutrients that have important health benefits,” she said.

“For colorectal cancer specifically, higher intakes of dietary fiber and whole grains have consistently been associated with lower risk,” Perelman noted.

“Therefore, rather than focusing exclusively on reducing fat, it is important to consider the overall dietary pattern and whether it provides adequate amounts of fiber-rich plant foods and other beneficial nutrients.”

Kirkpatrick agreed that the type of fat is what is important. “A Mediterranean-style diet that includes olive oil, nuts, seeds, and fatty fish can be relatively high in fat but is consistently associated with positive health outcomes,” she said.

“On the other hand, a diet high in saturated fat, processed meats, and ultra-processed foods may increase the risk of certain chronic diseases, particularly when it’s also low in fiber and other protective nutrients.”

Kirkpatrick also noted that many lifestyle habits contribute to a person’s overall health.

“Our health is influenced by so many factors beyond diet, including how we manage stress, our sleep habits, physical activity, genetics, and overall lifestyle,” she said.

#4614. A rare U.S. coin shouldn’t exist. It could auction for $2 million.

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 16, 2026 4:45 PM EST

One of the rarest and most coveted coins in United States history is headed for the auction block this week, where it could sell for over $2 million. But while collectors have long dreamed about owning one of the five existing 1885 silver trade dollars, the strange story of their creation remains murky more than 140 years after their minting

The U.S. struck the first trade dollars in 1873 as a way to compete with similar silver coinage in East Asia, but the production was short-lived. Silver market fluctuations and foreign policy shifts led to their demonetization in 1876, and they were only minted for collectors beginning in 1879. By 1884, the U.S. commissioned only 10 trade dollars before finally retiring the series destroying the die casts.

However, a thoroughly corrupt political appointee named A. Loudon Snowden had other plans. Snowden’s career in currencies began in 1857, when his uncle and former Treasurer of Pennsylvania hired the then 22-year-old whippersnapper at the Philadelphia Mint. While at the mint, he pursued various personal profiteering interests, including the clandestine production and selling of thousands of rare coins for collectors.In 1885, Snowden finally retired as Superintendent of the Philadelphia Mint after nearly three decades.

Snowden also gave himself a parting gift before retiring—five 1885 trade dollars that he purchased from the Mint cashier. No one knew of their existence until a year after Snowden’s death in 1912. The first 1885 trade dollar auctioned in 1913 for $1,140 (about $32,174 in current valuation).

Although some numismatists and historians argue Snowden’s five trade dollars were a final grift, other experts argue that the coins have a surprisingly mundane backstory. Until the 1930’s, Mint employees were legally allowed to purchase examples of new coinage for their equivalent amount. Snowden did just this when he previously bought 10 proof 1884 trade dollars, and it’s possible he bought the following year’s coins before the decision not to mint any others. Regardless of the true story, only five 1885 trade dollars exist today—and they’re worth far more than Snowden could ever imagine.

Stack’s Bowers will auction the 1885 trade dollar as part of its Rarities Night series on Tuesday, November 17.

Update 11/18/2026 12:50 p.m. EST: Stack’s Bowers confirmed its 1885 trade dollar sold for just over $1.95 million.

#4613. Lived Experience and Epistemic Privilege

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 22, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

"Ich habe Lebenserfahrung [I have life experience]."—E. Rudolf Krüger, putting his son in his place

"Experience keeps a dear school, but fools will learn in no other."—Benjamin Franklin, 1743, meditating on the benefits of heeding advice

A current trend in the psychological scene is seeking to rehabilitate lived experience as an element of scholarship (Krueger, 2026). The importance of lived experience as part of the human condition is undeniable (Casey, 2023). It is also undeniable that there is value in sampling reports of lived experience widely to ensure that a broad spectrum of voices is being heard; indeed, there is also value in oversampling voices from small populations to ensure that minority views are not drowned out by a majority din (Kalsbeek, 2003).

There are good reasons to think, however, that a chorus of voices will not amount to scholarship unless it is tamed, disciplined, and critically examined. Scientific methods can do this. They impose standards on the collection, the organization, and the interpretation of evidence (Godwin & Goodwin, 2016). Although stories and narratives are obligatory elements of the human condition (Gottschall, 2012), they cannot replace science; they can only be objects of scientific study. Stories are data, that is, material to be curated by theory and explored with standardized methodology. The idea that stories of lived experience can stand on their own is as mistaken as the idea that quantitative data, and especially “big data,” reveal reality all by themselves, without help from or intervention by a theoretically minded intellect (Felin et al., 2021).

Sir Karl Popper (1963) made this point jokingly. Beginning in 1928, he invited his students to “observe,” and when they asked, "What?" Popper exclaimed, "Aha!" Observation needs guidance. Then, the act of making an observation can create value; indeed, it can bring forth a reality, but only inasmuch as the observation is embedded in a web of expectations, knowledge, and prior experience. A phenomenologist might say that the lived experience of sensing and perceiving is the thing: It is Kant’s (1783) Ding an sich. We do not perceive a reality that is out there; instead, having a sensory experience is the reality.

Important as they are, it is doubtful that lived experiences can supersede systematic scientific work. Yet, stories and narratives populate the literature. How do they get in? One pathway is for everyone so inclined to write up their story and get it published. This genre of literature exists. When asked, the AI engine Claude estimates the number of published biographies to exceed 10,000 annually. A search of the term "Google n-gram viewer" shows that during the post-WWII era, the term “memoir” has risen in popularity, in tandem with the term self-esteem, suggesting a cultural drift to greater concern with the individual self. Yet, the term "memoir" already enjoyed an earlier flowering during the era of romanticism (see Figure 1).

To see how stories and narratives of lived experience enter the psychological literature, we have to look to the pathways offered by the field of qualitative psychology. Here, an increasingly popular view is that both the conductors of qualitative research and their informants gain epistemic privilege from lived experience relevant to the subject matter at hand (Levitt & Pierorazio, 2026). This view is critical of investigative neutrality, a traditional value of the scientific mindset. Thomas Nagel (1986) referred to this mindset when asking whether we can take “a view from nowhere,” a perspective which privileges no one (also, Weber, 1904; 1917).

Of course, the lived experience of informants is critical when it underlies the expertise that needs to be brought to the investigation. When researching, for example, what the experience of post-traumatic stress is like, informants must be found who have had that experience. Insisting that researchers ought to have had that same type of experience would be an odd demand. At best, an investigator’s lived experience is irrelevant; at worst, it sets the stage for methodological bias.

The terms of lived experience and epistemic privilege are increasingly seen in the literature, as shown by the second n-gram graph (Figure 2). The relative popularity of the term epistemic privilege seems to be lagging, perhaps because this term is more difficult to comprehend. One reason for this difficulty is that the term has been used in more than one way. One usage is to refer to a knowledgeable person who has privileged access to the material under investigation. To the early school of introspective psychology, pioneered by Wilhelm Wundt, privileged access to one’s own mental contents was the foundation of their scientific efforts. A very different way of referring to epistemic privilege is political (e.g., Hartsock, 1983). Here, the position of the researcher is called into question (or “interrogated”) as a source of bias or perhaps even oppressive intent. Wundt is turned on his head.

Many authors feel strongly about critically assessing researchers’ epistemic privilege. Alas, limiting access to research outlets because of concerns regarding the researcher’s positionality sets up a slippery slope that can lead to unwarranted exclusion. It is worthwhile asking whether psychological science is not best served by an ethos of epistemic neutrality. Let the quality and rigor of the research speak for itself. This ethic allows authors of different positionality and authors with different kinds of epistemic privilege—or lack thereof—to contribute to the conversation. Authors in the progressive vein, for example, may wish to recall that from Marx to Lenin and to the Frankfurt School, the most influential authors emerged from the bourgeoisie. Should they have been denied the privilege of championing the interests of the proletariat?

My sympathies lie with the conventional ethic of blind reception. Let the research speak for itself, and let it be evaluated in light of explicit, rigorous, and shared standards. In my teaching, though, I seek to help students situate individual research articles within the authors’ life’s work. When students give a presentation in class, I ask them to include a short author biography with key data from their career and even a photo if they can find one. This exercise helps students understand why the researchers care about their work and see connections across studies. The goal is not to “interrogate” the researchers’ motives or use their demographic data as grounds for speculation about their intentions.

Robust scientific results should stand regardless of who produced them. In time, memory for findings should crystallize, while memory for the authors’ identity should suffer the fate of source amnesia. May the findings last—if they are true and replicable—while the finders’ identities fade.

Casey, P. J. (2023). Lived experience: Defined and critiqued. Critical Horizons, 24, 282-297.

Felin, T., Koenderink, J., Krueger, J. I., Noble, D., & Ellis, G. (2021b). Data bias. Genome Biology, 22:59

Franklin, B. (1743/1961). Poor Richard, 1743. In L. W. Labaree (Ed.), The papers of Benjamin Franklin (Vol. 2, pp. 337-350). Yale University Press.

Goodwin, K. A., & Goodwin, C. J. (2016). Research in psychology: Methods and design (8th ed.). Wiley.

Gottschall, J. (2012). The storytelling animal: How stories make us human. Houghton Mifflin.

Hartsock, N. C. M. (1983). The feminist standpoint: Developing the ground for a specifically feminist historical materialism. In S. Harding & M. B. Hintikka (eds.), Discovering reality (pp. 283-310). Reidel.

Kalsbeek, W. D. (2003). Sampling minority groups in health surveys. Statistics in Medicine 22, 1527–1549.

Kant, I. (1783). Prolegomena zu einer jeden künftigen Metaphysik, die als Wissenschaft wird auftreten können [Prolegomena to any future metaphysics that will be able to come forward as a science]. Johann Friedrich Hartknoch.

Krueger, J. I. (2026). Are you experienced? Psychology Today Online. https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/one-among-many/202611/are-you-experienced

Levitt, H. M., & Pierorazio, N. A. (2026). A methodological justification of positionality and reflexivity reflections: Why, how, and when they increase methodological integrity. Theory & Psychology. DOI: 10.1177/09593543261474437

Nagel, T. (1986). The view from nowhere. Oxford University Press.

Popper, K. R. (1963). Conjectures and refutations: The growth of scientific knowledge. Routledge.

Weber, M. (1904). Die "Objektivität" sozialwissenschaftlicher und sozialpolitischer Erkenntnis [Objectivity in social science and social policy]. Archiv für Sozialwissenschaft und Sozialpolitik, 19, 22-87.

Weber, M. (1917). Der Sinn der "Wertfreiheit" der soziologischen und ökonomischen Wissenschaften [The meaning of "value freedom" in the sociological and economic sciences]. Logos: Internationale Zeitschrift für Philosophie der Kultur, 7, 40-88.
